activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The festival had spread itself across the park in tents of every color, and Nathan stood at the edge of it holding his debate notes in a folder he had bent into a soft curl at the corners. His event was in forty minutes, in the community tent, and the resolution was one he had drawn at random: whether an ancient religious rule still binds people who no longer live in the world that made it. Mr. Hernández had told him, the week before, that the only defensible way to argue it was from the text itself, not from what people said about the text. "Everyone interpolates their own politics into scripture," his coach had said, tapping the photocopied page. "Your job is to quote it cold and let it sit there." Nathan had nodded then, in the classroom with its smell of dry-erase markers, and only now, under the festival loudspeakers, did he understand how hard that would be to actually do.

He found Leena at the falafel table, wearing the volunteer shirt she had been assigned, handing out samples with a wooden pick. She had agreed to be his practice audience. They sat on a hay bale near the craft tent, and he opened the folder, though he already knew the verse by heart. "Leviticus 19:9 and 10," he said. "It commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields, but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings, for the poor and the stranger."

"So it's about farming," Leena said, which was exactly the question he was dreading, because it was the question the judges would ask. "Nobody here farms. Half this park used to be a peach orchard and now it's a splash pad."

That was true, and Nathan said so, and then found himself arguing the other side without having decided to, almost to see what it felt like. A rule about corners, he said, was a rule about edges, about the part of your work you were entitled to and the part you weren't. The farmer still owned the field. The command didn't confiscate anything; it just drew a line and said the line was not where you thought it was. Leena bit into her own sample, considering, and said that sounded like a sermon, like one of those bromides people print on coffee mugs, feed the poor, be kind, and she wanted to know what he would actually do about it, on a street with no fields anywhere.

Jazmine rescued him, or complicated him, by arriving with a paper plate of dumplings and the announcement that the community tent had a microphone problem, that the debate might start late, that a woman at the information booth wanted volunteers to carry folding chairs. Nathan carried chairs. Between trips he kept turning the verse over. The stranger, not only the poor; that phrase kept snagging on something. He remembered being nine at his grandfather's retirement party, standing at the edge of the buffet while adults he didn't know filled their plates, and how a cousin of his grandfather's had waved him forward and cut the corner off a sheet cake for him before the speeches were done, and how his mother had later called it rude, taking from the corners early. He had not thought about that in years, and he still didn't know which of the two adults had been right, and the not knowing felt honest in a way he couldn't yet use.

While the sound man tested the microphone with a word that boomed and dropped out, Leena texted him, since the tent was too big for shouting: "judges are 2 college kids and a rabbi from the temple booth. The rabbi has a gleaning poster. Watch out." Nathan read it twice. A poster meant the rabbi knew the verse better than he did, knew the whole landscape around it, and for a moment he considered softening his case, hedging every claim, the way you do when the room knows more than you. But Mr. Hernández's voice came back to him, quoting cold, letting it sit, and he decided instead to put his uncertainty in the middle of the speech where the judges would have to look at it.

When his turn came, the microphone finally holding, Nathan laid out the verse plainly, the corners and the gleanings, the poor and the stranger, and then said what the street with no fields had forced him to say. He did not know whether the rule survived by analogy or by translation, whether leaving your corner meant tipping twenty percent or simply not reaping every advantage available to you, and he suspected anyone who claimed certainty was selling something. What he did know, standing there, was that the verse assumed abundance and asked for restraint at the edge of it, and that a splash pad was not a field but a person was still a person with edges. The college judges wrote nothing. The rabbi stopped writing too, and looked up at him for a long moment, and Nathan felt something shift in him that was small and quiet and seismic at once, the way a level finds its bubble.

Afterward the rabbi found him by the hay bales, poster rolled under one arm, and asked whether he had ever been the stranger at the edge of a field himself. Nathan said he thought maybe once, at a buffet, a long time ago. Leena, listening, laughed, and Jazmine said, "That's your closing line next time, obviously," and the rabbi unrolled the poster against the bale and pointed at the painted corner of a painted field, cut open, unreaped, and asked, "So tell me. What is your corner?"

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
Aaron's mother had cleared the kitchen table of everything except two mugs and the laminated study sheet from the driving school, and she kept glancing at it as though the diagrams of cones and curbs might rearrange themselves if she looked away long enough. Aaron sat across from her with a slice of toast going cold in his hand. Parallel parking, the sheet said, was the most failed portion of the road test in their jurisdiction, and his test was in nine days.

"The neighbours will think we've lost it," his mother said, but she was already pulling on her coat. Ms. Zhou had offered her driveway, which was wide and empty in the afternoons, and had even produced a pair of plastic cones from her garage, faded orange and slightly friable at the tips, so that squeezing them meant leaving little crumbs of bright dust on the pavement. Ms. Zhou stood at the edge of the driveway with her arms folded, watching Aaron attempt the manoeuvre for the sixth time.

"You're turning too early," she said. "Back up straight until your rear bumper is level with the front cone, then turn hard." She had driven trucks for twenty years before retiring, she'd told him, and she had opinions about how cars ought to be handled. Aaron tried again. The tyres climbed the curb with a scrape that made his shoulders bunch.

At school, Makenzie had failed her own test the previous month on parallel parking alone, and she'd described the experience with a flatness that Aaron found more frightening than weeping would have been. "The examiner just wrote something down," she said at lunch, "and that was it. I didn't even get to finish the route." Tracy, who had passed on the first try, offered the opposite wisdom, which was that the whole test was a matter of confidence, that the examiner could smell hesitation. Between the two of them, Aaron couldn't decide whether the test was a technical problem or a character problem, and he suspected the answer mattered.

He practised every evening that week. Ms. Zhou stood in the same spot each time, calling corrections in a voice that carried. By Thursday he could settle the car between the cones in three moves, then two. His mother watched from the kitchen window while she washed dishes, and when he came inside she would hand him tea without comment, which he understood to be praise.

The highway portion fell to the driving school instructor, a heavy man who rode with his window cracked open in every weather. On the entrance ramp, Aaron accelerated toward a gap behind a white sedan, but a transport truck sat in the right lane beside him, and Aaron waited, easing off, certain the truck would drift left to let him in. The speed limit was a hundred and the ramp was shortening under them.

"Who has to move here?" the instructor asked. "You or him?" Aaron looked at the truck's mirrored flank and understood, in one cold drop, that the answer was him. "Traffic already on the highway has the right of way," the instructor said. "You fit the gap. You don't wait for people to make one." Aaron pressed the accelerator, found the gap behind the sedan, and slid into the flow of cars so smoothly that the steering wheel barely turned. His hands were shaking anyway, and he kept them high on the wheel where the shaking would be less visible.

That night he sat at the kitchen table with the study sheet pushed aside and tried to reconcile the two afternoons, the driveway and the ramp, but the pieces wouldn't line up cleanly. In the parking exercise, the world was supposed to accommodate him, the cones and the curb simply there, immovable, and his job was to shape his movements around fixed objects. On the ramp, everything moved, and the law itself took the other drivers' side. He thought of Tracy saying confidence, of Makenzie saying the examiner just wrote something down, and of Ms. Zhou's voice on the driveway, and he noticed that his mother had stopped hovering over the sheet. She was peeling an orange at the counter, and the smell of it filled the kitchen.

He couldn't make the two ideas into one neat principle, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it. Perhaps the test would demand the parking mind, perhaps the merging mind, perhaps some third mind he hadn't yet met. What he knew was smaller and firmer than any theory: when he stopped expecting the world to clear a path and began reading the traffic for his own opening, the car had gone where he wanted it to go. He folded the study sheet once, twice, and set it under the fruit bowl.

On the morning of the test, Ms. Zhou was already outside, dragging the cones into position along her curb. She raised one hand as he backed out of the driveway. "Signal first," she called.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
The crystals sat in a jar on the kitchen counter, blue and sharp-edged, and Logan had promised Ms. Johansson a poster by Monday that would explain, in her words, "where the numbers went." The numbers had gone somewhere. He had started with a weighed amount of copper sulfate powder, done the arithmetic three times, and predicted a mass of crystal that the jar did not contain. Somewhere between the powder and the jar, four grams had simply left.

He spread his notebook beside the toaster. First the part he understood: grams of reactant, divided by molar mass, gave moles, and moles told you, in that patient bookkeeping way chemistry had, how much product you were owed. One mole of copper sulfate weighed about two hundred fifty grams; he had measured out fifty, which was a fifth of a mole, which entitled him to a fifth of a mole of crystal. He had written it all out on Saturday with the seriousness of a person balancing a checkbook, and Saturday Logan had been confident. Sunday Logan was staring at a scale that said otherwise.

His mother came through in her work uniform, looked at the jar, and asked if the blue stuff was going to ferment or if it just sat there. He said it just sat there. She said in that case it was the quietest science project the kitchen had ever hosted, and she took the car keys off the hook by the door and left for her shift.

Crystal arrived at four with a bag of chips and no sympathy. She leaned over his notebook, chewing, and read his prediction aloud. "Twirteen grams theoretical. And you got, what, nine point something?"

"Nine point four."

"So you lost three point six grams of nothing. That's not even a thing you can lose." She tapped the jar. "Unless it is, and you just don't know what it's called."

Ms. Johansson had used a phrase on Friday that Logan had written in the margin precisely because he didn't understand it, the way you save a word you intend to look up and then don't. He found the margin now. Next to it he had doodled a crown, which at the time had seemed grandiose enough to match the phrase, and now just looked like a crown.

"Percent yield," Crystal read, mouth full. "Is that a real thing or did you make it up?"

He looked at it, and then at the scale, and then at his Saturday arithmetic, which had never been wrong, only incomplete. The theoretical yield was what the moles said he was owed. The actual yield was what the scale said he got. If percent yield meant anything, it meant putting those two numbers in the same sentence and letting them argue. He took the calculator off the counter, the one his mother used for the grocery budget, and divided nine point four by thirteen. Zero point seven two something. Times a hundred.

"Seventy-two percent," he said.

"Out of what?"

"Out of perfect. Out of what the math said I should have." He wrote it under the theoretical line, and the two figures sat there together, one concrete and one not, and neither one apologized for the other. Seventy-two percent was not a failure and not a success; it was a number that needed a home, and now it had one, on a poster with the jar next to it, blue and sharp and slightly underweight.

"Etymology of 'yield,'" Crystal said, apropos of nothing, because she was the sort of person who kept trivia the way other people kept lint. "It originally meant what you pay back. Like the land yields a crop."

"So the math is the land," Logan said, "and my jar is the crop."

"Your crop is short," she said. "Seventy-two percent of a crop." She took another chip and looked at the crystals with the expression of someone appraising a farmer's pumpkins at the county fair. Logan capped the jar and set it on the poster board, where it caught the light from the window over the sink and threw a small blue lozenge of it onto the linoleum.

He still didn't know where the missing grams had gone, and he wrote that on the poster too, at the bottom, in ordinary handwriting: where the rest went, unclear. Ms. Johansson would either like that or she wouldn't. Crystal finished the chips, folded the bag into a small triangle, and pointed at the jar.

"So Monday, you stand there and tell a judge your crystals came up short."

"Seventy-two percent short of perfect," Logan said. "I'm leading with that."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lea stood in her aunt's backyard with a plastic bag of old newspapers and a question she had not managed to ask anyone yet. The pile of wood in the middle of the lawn was already taller than her uncle, stacked with branches and cardboard and a broken chair leg, and around it her cousins were circling like slow planets. Her mother had told her that morning, in the flat voice she used for family obligations, that they would go. Lea had said fine. She had not said that she'd had plans for the evening, or that Grayden was holding two tickets to something she would now miss.

She began feeding the newspapers into the gaps between branches, because her hands needed something to do. The paper was mostly her old schoolwork, saved for burning, and she recognized a chemistry quiz with a red 61 at the top before she tucked it in. Her little cousin ran past with a packet of colored powder held above his head like contraband, saving it, everyone knew, for the morning, when the streets would turn into something seismic and orange and unbearable.

"You know why tonight is tonight?" her uncle asked, not really asking, the way adults opened conversations they intended to finish themselves. But Lea's cousin Alina, who had come early and claimed the good chair, answered first. "Holika Dahan," Alina said. "The bonfire. It's the night before the colors." She said it the way she said most things, lightly, as though the words cost her nothing, and Lea was grateful and slightly annoyed at once, because now she couldn't ask without admitting she hadn't known.

Her uncle went on anyway, warming to it, and Lea listened while pretending to arrange the newspapers. Holi fell on the full moon of the month Phalguna, he said, which landed in March this year, the way it usually did. Tomorrow the colors, tonight the fire. He liked the sequence of it, the burning before the brightness. Lea filed the details away carefully, the way she studied before an exam she intended to actually understand, because there was something in her that wanted to get it right.

She had been getting it wrong for years, she realized, standing there. Not the facts, which she could have looked up in thirty seconds. She had decided at some point that the whole apparatus of it, the prayers and the fires and the relatives arriving in waves, was her mother's world, adjacent to hers, tolerable the way weather is tolerable. And she had also decided, separately, that this was a reasonable position for a person who was leaving for college in August. Two decisions that didn't quite touch each other. She noticed this the way you notice a door left open in a house you thought you'd checked.

Her grandmother came out with a plate of something sweet, and the relatives gathered, and the fire was lit as the sky went from grey to a deeper grey that was almost purple. The flames took the old quiz first, then the branches, then the broken chair leg, and Lea watched the heat bend the air above the pile so that the fence behind it seemed to ripple. Her little cousin had stopped running and stood transfixed, his packet of powder forgotten in his hand, his face lit orange from below.

Grayden texted again. She looked at the phone, at the fire, at Alina laughing at something their uncle had said. She thought about Alina saying Holika Dahan so easily, as though naming a thing and belonging to it were unrelated acts, and she thought about her own half-belonging, the way she could recite the calendar but not the feeling. Maybe the two were the same thing, maybe they weren't. She held both possibilities the way she held the phone, lightly, without deciding.

She typed that she wasn't coming, sorry, tomorrow instead. Then she put the phone in her pocket and moved closer to the fire, where her mother stood with her arms crossed against the last of the March cold, and Lea stood beside her without saying anything, and the two of them watched the full moon come up over the roofline, pale and unbothered, while the bonfire cracked and spat sparks into the dark.

"You'll ruin that jacket," her mother said.

"I know," said Lea, and stayed where she was.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
The paycheque was thinner than David had promised himself it would be. He stood at the till of the hardware store with the envelope half-open in his hand, doing the arithmetic twice, because the second time had to come out different. He had worked ninety-one hours since June, and the number at the bottom of the stub, the one that had actually landed in his account, was smaller than ninety-one times his wage by a margin he could not explain away as a typo. The stub itself was patient with him. Gross pay, it said, and then a ladder of lines beneath: income tax, and after it two more deductions with initials instead of names, each shaving off its share before the net pay at the bottom, which was the only number the bank cared about.

"That's the government's cut," Ms. Brown said from behind the service desk, not looking up from the schedule she was pencilling. "First cheque always stings. You get some of the income tax back when you file your return, if you made as little as you think you did." She said it the way she said most things, flat and practical, and David folded the stub into his back pocket where it could not keep staring at him.

He had been saving for a laptop, the one hinge-flecked machine that would carry him through first year without his mother absorbing the cost, and the shortfall on the cheque mattered in a concrete, September-shaped way. That afternoon Zoey came in for sandpaper and waited while he rang her up. "Why does the receipt only have one tax line?" she asked, squinting at the slip. "Back home in Montreal the bills show two." David looked at the printout. There it was, a single line, HST, thirteen percent, folded into the total as if it had always belonged there.

"Harmonized Sales Tax," said Alaina, who had trailed in after Zoey and was leaning on the counter with a slushie. "I looked it up after my first restaurant bill here nearly broke me." David turned the receipt over, then pulled another from the bin beside the register and laid them side by side. So Ontario had taken the federal GST and the provincial sales tax and combined them, one rate, one line, no seam showing. He had been mentally adding a second tax the whole summer, budgeting like the receipt was going to ambush him at the end, and it had been simpler than he feared. It was a strange relief, being wrong in the direction of less complication.

The wrongness of his other assumption did not dissolve so easily. He remembered April, the kitchen table covered in his father's tax return, receipts fanned out like cards from a lost hand. His father had kept every bus pass, every pharmacy slip, hunting through them for deductions, and when David asked why he bothered for amounts that seemed small, his father said that small was how it added up, and that a return was just the year telling you what you actually owed after everything was counted. David had gone back to his room then, uninterested. Now he sat in the break room with his own stub on his knee and his father's shoebox of a life suddenly legible, and he understood that the box of receipts and the ladder of lines on his paycheque were the same conversation held months apart.

The conversation was interrupted by the alarm at the door. A man in a grey jacket was halfway to the parking lot with a cordless drill still tagged, moving fast, and David did not think; he was through the gate and after him, past Ms. Brown's voice saying his name in a tone he would hear again that evening. The man dropped the drill at the curb and kept going, deciding apparently that a hundred and sixty dollars was not worth the risk of being caught absconding with it, and David stood in the exhaust-smelling heat holding the box while the drill's case, impermeable to everything the afternoon could throw at it, gleamed unbothered in his hands.

Ms. Brown did not shout at him. She took the drill, told him the store carried insurance for exactly this, that the policy's indemnity meant the loss would be covered whether or not he played hero, and that next year, when he was older and theoretically wiser, she expected him to let the man run. "You could have been hurt over a drill," she said. "Do the math on that." Then, softer, because she had seen the stub: "Bring your return questions to me in March. I've done thirty of them."

That evening David laid the paycheque stub and Zoey's receipt side by side on his desk, next to the laptop page he had bookmarked. One document showed what the province took when he spent; the other, what the governments took when he earned. He did not yet know how the two systems balanced against each other, or whether the refund Ms. Brown promised would arrive before the tuition deposit came due, and he wrote both uncertainties down in his phone instead of pretending they were settled. Then he texted his father a photograph of the stub, no caption, and watched the three dots appear and vanish and appear again. "Give me a call when you're off," the reply said. "We'll go through it." He pressed dial.

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The interview lasted six minutes. Ms. Zhang walked Luke through the lobby while the last matinee let out, past the smell of burnt caramel and the sticky patch near ticketing that nobody had mopped, and asked him three questions: his age, his availability, and whether he could work Christmas Eve. When he said yes to all three, she handed him a laminated sheet about training shifts and said, "You start Friday."

He texted Kaden from the bus stop. Kaden worked at the theater until October, and his reply came back fast: "congrats. dont make my mistakes." Luke had to wait until after dinner to walk to Kaden's house and find out what that meant.

Kaden was morose about it in the way he got morose about everything now, lying on his bed with his phone held above his face. He had walked out of the theater on a Saturday night, mid-shift, because a manager had yelled at him over a spilled ICEE and because he hated the job in a way that had been building for months. He hadn't given notice. He'd just left. "They didn't even call me after," Kaden said. "Nobody called. I thought I'd get some warning letter or whatever. Nothing."

"So what happened?"

"Nothing happened. That's the point." Kaden sat up. "My cousin looked it up. Most jobs here are at-will. Means the employer or the worker can end the job at any time, for any reason that isn't illegal. They could've fired me any day they wanted. I could've quit any day I wanted. That's the whole deal."

Luke turned that over on the walk home, past the gas station and the darkened strip mall. It bothered him in a way he couldn't immediately name. Part of him admired Kaden's exit, the cleanliness of it, the refusal to grovel. Another part remembered Kaden in September, before the walkout, complaining but still saving for a car, still with a plan. The freedom to leave in an instant and the freedom to be left in an instant were, it turned out, the same freedom, and Luke wasn't sure he wanted to hold it the way Kaden had. He'd always liked systems you could reason your way through, a small private rationalism about how things worked, and this was a system with almost no structure to reason about. No contract, no promises. Just two people who could each walk away.

On Friday he arrived twenty minutes early and found Ms. Zhang behind the concession counter, counting cups. She put him on popcorn. The machine had its own logic, the oil and the kernels and the exact moment the lid went on, and by the second hour his arms smelled of salt and his ears had adjusted to the rumble of projector five through the wall. At one point a customer threw a napkin at him because the butter pump had clogged, and Luke felt a hot flare of exactly what Kaden must have felt, the sudden urge to sequester himself in the supply room or just keep walking out the back door and never come back.

He didn't. He fixed the pump, filled the order, and when the rush thinned, Ms. Zhang appeared beside him with a clipboard. "You're faster than the last two," she said. "The last two walked out." She said it lightly, but not entirely. She counted a drawer and didn't look at him while she said it, which was how he understood that it had cost her something, the constant leaving, the Friday hires who evaporated by Sunday.

They stood together at the counter, the lobby quiet now, the smell of popcorn settling into everything, the floor still tacky underfoot. Luke thought about telling her what he'd decided, that he'd stay through Christmas, that he wasn't going to be the last two, but he caught himself. He didn't know yet whether he could promise it, and he'd rather not say the words than say them and dissolve them. At-will meant his staying was a choice he'd have to keep making, shift by shift, without a contract to hold him or excuse him. That seemed, honestly, like more than he could guarantee anybody tonight.

Ms. Zhang snapped the clipboard under her arm. "Six to close tomorrow," she said. "Bring a hair tie."

"Yes, ma'am," Luke said, and went back to the popcorn machine, scooping the fresh batch into a warm red bucket.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
story:
The interview was supposed to take ten minutes, but Mr. Kim kept sliding cups down the counter, talking to Leo between orders, so that by the time he offered the job the afternoon had gone soft and torpid, the lunch rush thinning to a few people hunched over laptops. Saturdays and Sundays, eight hours each, starting immediately. Money Leo needed if he was going to fix the car before September, and the car was the difference between commuting to the community college and living on a campus four hours away.

"You don't have to answer today," Mr. Kim said, wiping the steam wand. "But I need someone by Friday. Small shop, small margin. I can't hold the position."

Leo said he'd think about it, which he already knew was a way of not saying no. On the table in front of him lay the paperback he'd been reading while he waited, its spine cracked nearly in half. Mr. Kim glanced at it.

"The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress," he read off the cover. "My brother gave me that when I came to this country. Where do you think 'There ain't no such thing as a free lunch' comes from? People say it like it fell out of the sky. It was popularized by that book. Heinlein, 1966."

"Popularized," Leo repeated. "So not invented there."

"Invented somewhere, spread everywhere." Mr. Kim shrugged. "Same as most things we think we thought of ourselves."

That night, a message from Brenden lit up Leo's phone screen, and he read it three times before answering. It was longer than Brenden usually wrote, which meant he'd been drafting it, deleting, drafting again. "So my uncle got the tickets after all," it read. "Both nights of the festival, camping pass included, the whole thing. I know you said the job thing might happen. But this is the last summer before everything scatters, and I've been thinking about how the summers we get aren't infinite, and honestly the ones that feel infinite already happened, we just didn't notice while they were happening. My uncle says we'd leave the fifth. Let me know. Either way, no hard feelings, but there would be hard feelings, a little."

Leo typed and deleted four replies. He walked to the window. Down the street, a banner outside the new tea place read FREE BOBA WITH SURVEY, and a line had formed anyway, people waiting to trade ten minutes of their lives for six ounces of sweetened milk. Nothing about the exchange looked unfair. Everyone in line seemed pleased with themselves. And yet the phrase from Mr. Kim kept circling back, not because the boba cost money but because it cost something. He didn't have the word for it, so he tried to build one. What you give up. The next thing you would have done instead. His economics teacher had once scrawled a term on the board in September, something with "cost" in it, and Leo had let the memory calcify into a vague association with graphs and supply curves instead of an idea he might actually need.

Mackenna found him at the coffee shop the next afternoon, doing the trial shift Mr. Kim had suggested before deciding. She ordered a cappuccino she didn't want and sat at the counter watching him steam milk badly.

"Word travels," she said. "Brenden told me about the festival before he even texted you, which, by the way, is a whole other conversation. Have you decided?"

"If I take the job, I fix the car by October. Maybe campus housing in spring semester." He set down the pitcher. "If I go to the festival, I get two nights and a drive up the coast with Brenden, and I don't fix the car, and I tell Mr. Kim no after I already said maybe."

"That's not a decision, that's a list."

"It's a list where both sides have real things on them. That's the problem. Everybody talks like choices are between a good thing and a bad thing, but it's never that. It's a good thing and a different good thing, and you pay for one with the other." He heard himself and almost laughed. "Brenden would say I'm being pretentious."

Mackenna stirred her untouched cappuccino. "My dad calls that the free lunch thing. Says it at dinner constantly. Nothing's free, everything costs." She paused. "He also once spent a deposition week testifying in a lawsuit instead of my grandmother's eightieth birthday, and he still brings it up every time the cake comes out. So maybe know that the invoice doesn't always arrive on schedule. Sometimes you find out what something cost years later."

Leo worked the Sunday after that, and the Sunday after, because on Saturday morning he drove with Brenden up the coast instead, the two of them sleeping in the car at a rest stop when the campsite fell through, arriving at the festival just as the first night ended, standing at the fence in the dark listening to a band they'd paid to see play without them. It was, Leo thought, half of what he'd chosen, delivered at half strength, and he still wouldn't have traded it, and he still couldn't say why with any confidence. On the drive home, Brenden asleep against the window, Leo passed the exit for Mr. Kim's shop and calculated that three weekends of missed shifts equaled the brake job, maybe, if nothing else went wrong with the car. The numbers sat in his chest the way numbers do when they're also something else.

Mr. Kim gave the weekend position to someone else but offered Leo two weeknight shifts, which was a kindness disguised as scheduling, and Leo said thank you and meant it and knew it wasn't the same. In September the car ran, barely, and the campus was four hours away after all. On his last night at the shop before moving, Mr. Kim slid a bag of coffee beans across the counter, no charge, and Leo looked at it for a long second before taking it.

"There ain't no such thing," Leo said, and grinned.

"This one's from the wrong supplier," Mr. Kim said. "It costs me nothing."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
The market opened at seven, and by half past, the white tents threw their shadows across the gravel like a forewarning of the afternoon heat, adumbrating the slow wilt of lettuce and the softening of every butter-based thing on every table. Hannah had arrived earlier than all of it, carrying a cooler with three pounds of couverture and a notebook in which she had written, the night before, the words shine and snap, underlined twice, as though underlining could substitute for skill.

Her stall, such as it was, sat at the end of the row between Mr. Wijaya's stone fruit and a beekeeper from two towns over. She had paid for the spot with the last of her birthday money on the theory that people who came for peaches and honey might also want a bar of chocolate, provided the chocolate looked like something worth wanting. The bars she had made in her own kitchen did not. They were dull, streaked grey in places, and when she had broken one for Kayden, it had bent with a soft, apologetic sound instead of breaking, and Kayden had eaten it anyway and said nothing, which was its own kind of verdict.

"You're set up next to the only man in the county with a marble counter in his truck," Kayden said, arriving with Caroline close behind, both of them still carrying the smell of the parking lot. "I checked. It's for the fruit, so nothing bruises, but still."

Mr. Wijaya's truck had a slab of pale marble laid across the bed, cool to the touch even in July, and Hannah had noticed it the way you notice a solution before you understand the problem. In her notebook, below shine and snap, she had copied a line from a library book: melted chocolate spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming. She had not fully believed it. It sounded like folklore, like something passed down rather than discovered.

"It's called tabling," she said to Caroline, who was reading over her shoulder without shame. "That's the word for it. The spreading part."

"You're going to do it here?" Caroline picked up one of the failed bars and turned it over, and the grey bloom on its surface caught the light badly. "In public, where people can watch you fail?"

"That's the idea." Hannah had already carried a bowl of melted chocolate across the gravel to Mr. Wijaya's truck, and he had looked at her, and at the bowl, and had moved a basket of plums aside without a word, which she took for permission. He was a neighbor from three streets down, the kind of man who had watched her grow up without ever once asking her a question she couldn't answer, and she found his silence more useful than encouragement would have been.

She poured a puddle of chocolate onto the marble. It sat there, glossy and slow. She spread it with the flat of a spatula, scraped it back toward the center, spread it again, and the slab pulled the heat out of it visibly, the gloss going matte at the edges and then, as she worked it, the whole mass tightening, thickening, beginning to behave like something with intentions. Caroline had drifted over from the stall. Even Kayden, who had spent the whole ride to the market explaining his new philosophy survey course and the word nihilism, whether nothing mattered or whether the nothing was what mattered, had stopped mid-sentence. "Wait," he said. "It's changing. You can see it changing."

"It's working," Hannah said, and then, because she was honest with herself even when it cost something, "I think it's working. I don't know yet. You don't know until it sets." She gathered it back into the bowl with the scraper, fast now, before it could harden on the slab, and carried it to the molds she had lined up on her own folding table. The beekeeper wandered past, offered them each a taste of honey from a comb, and remarked that his bees were autochthonous to the valley, born there and staying there, unlike everybody else under these tents, himself included. Caroline asked him what that word meant and he told her, and Hannah filed it away beside tabling in the part of her mind where words that meant real things went to live.

While the molds sat in the shade, Hannah counted the morning's customers, which took very little time. Two people had bought the failed bars at a dollar each, out of pity or politeness. A woman had asked whether the chocolate was local, and Hannah had said no, cocoa doesn't grow here, and the woman had moved on. Hannah thought about the bakery in town where she had worked last spring, where the owner had offered to teach her this exact thing, proper tempering, real technique, and where Hannah had quit in June over a schedule conflict that had not, in hindsight, actually been a conflict. She had told herself at the time that she wanted to learn it on her own terms. She was no longer certain those terms existed.

"Can I break one?" Kayden was standing over the first mold, which had gone quiet and flat, and the surface of it, where it met the plastic, looked like a lake at dawn. He said it the way he said things he already knew the answer to.

She tipped the bar out into her palm. It came free with a sound like a small door unlatching, and the top of it shone, really shone, and she held it out without a word, and Kayden snapped a corner off and the sound was clean, a click, and nothing streaked or bent or apologized.

"Mr. Wijaya," Hannah called across the gravel, holding the bar up so the light ran down it. "Look."

He looked, and nodded once, and went back to his plums, and Hannah stood there turning the bar in her hand, unsure whether she had earned this or borrowed it, and knowing the molds still cooling would tell her which.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
I did not care about football, which is why I was the first one at Ms. Eze's house on the night of the championship, holding a bag of tortilla chips and standing in her doorway while she found room on the counter between the crock pot and a bowl of something involving artichokes. I was there for the food, obviously, and because my mother said we had been invited and refusing would be rude, and because Coby had texted me four times asking if I was coming, in that order of importance. That I had worn my lucky socks, the red ones, was a coincidence of laundry.

Ms. Eze's living room filled up the way it always did, with my parents on the good couch, Kolton sprawled on the floor with his back against the coffee table, and Coby arriving last, loud, carrying a jersey he'd apparently bought on the walk over, tags still dangling from the collar. The TV was enormous and slightly too bright, so that the green of the field looked almost radioactive, and the whole room smelled like melted cheese and the lemon polish Ms. Eze used on her wood furniture. She had lived alone in that house since her husband died, and she liked a crowd, and she liked explaining her television's remote, which had an idiosyncrasy where the volume button only worked if you pressed it with a fingernail instead of a fingertip.

The game was close for three quarters, which meant everybody yelled, and I did not yell, I want that on the record. I sat in the armchair and ate chips with dignity. Then in the fourth quarter the quarterback, whose name I definitely knew before that night and did not have to read off Coby's phone, threw a long pass that hung in the air forever, and the receiver caught it at the two-yard line, and we scored on the next play and won by four.

Coby stood up so fast he knocked over his soda. "That's what I'm talking about! We won! We did it!" He was waving the jersey over his head like a flag. Kolton, who had money on the other team and had grown increasingly morose as the fourth quarter drained away, muttered something from the floor.

"We," I said. "Interesting word choice from a man who has never touched a football."

"I've thrown one."

"You've thrown one at a goose, Coby. At the pond. The goose won."

He laughed, but then he went strangely quiet, and Ms. Eze, wiping up the soda, said in an offhand way, "There's actually a famous study about exactly that," and then, before she could ruin my evening with a lecture, the doorbell rang and she went to answer it and never came back to the topic, because it was another neighbor with a casserole and an opinion about the halftime show.

I could not stop thinking about it, though, which is another way of saying I cared about something and pretended it was curiosity. While everyone argued about whether the refs had blown a call, I slipped into Ms. Eze's den, where she kept her old teaching books, and found a fat social psychology textbook with a cracked spine. The index sent me to a page about a 1976 study by a man named Cialdini, and there it was: after their football team won, students wore more clothing with the university's name on it. And when they described a win, they said "we," but for a loss, they said "they." I read it twice, standing there with one hip against her desk, smelling dust and the ghost of a thousand cups of coffee, and then I went back to the living room to conduct science.

Coby had put the jersey on. Over his shirt. Tags still on, I swear, sticking up at the back of his neck like a tiny white flag. Kolton, who had gone to the same university as the losing team for one semester before transferring, was not wearing any school apparel at all, and when my dad asked him about the game, he said, "They couldn't stop the run," and "They turned it over twice," and not once, in ten whole minutes of sulking, did he say we.

I stood by the counter with my chips, watching the room like a nature documentary. My father, alum, sweatshirt. My mother, alum by marriage, sweatshirt, borrowed. Coby in his tags. It was all right there, pinned like a butterfly, and I felt the smug warm glow of knowing a thing, and then, about five minutes later, I heard my own voice say, to Ms. Eze, "Did you see that catch we made?" and the glow curdled instantly. I had learned a fact about a bias and then performed the bias in the same half hour, which either made me a hypocrite or made me human, and I could not decide which, and I hated that I could not decide, and the not deciding lasted all the way through the dishes.

Walking home under the streetlights, Coby still in his jersey, Kolton trailing behind with his hands in his pockets, I told them about the study. Coby said, "So it's not just me, it's science," looking relieved, and Kolton said, "Whatever, I didn't even really go there," and then, quieter, after a block, "They never should have punted." I pulled my coat tighter. In my pocket, my fingers found the frayed cuff of my lucky socks, balled up and carried like a talisman, and I left them where they were.

"Same time next season?" Coby said.

"Only if Ms. Eze makes the artichoke thing," I said, and I meant we.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
story:
Benjamin had spread the county's flood maps across the kitchen table like evidence in a trial only he was attending. His mother kept moving his coffee mug to safer ground, which suggested she had opinions about the veracity of his organization system, though she said nothing. The assignment was Ms. Grant's: map flood risk against housing for the city, and say something worth saying about the two together.

The problem was the official flood zone. It followed the river in a tidy polygon, drawn years ago by people Benjamin pictured as cautious and well paid, and it excluded an awful lot of houses that sat close enough to the water to make him nervous on their behalf. He zoomed in on the east side, where the streets named after trees, Willow and Alder and Sycamore, ran parallel to the bank. Half of Alder Street sat outside the zone. All of Sycamore sat outside it. He did not believe in the polygon.

He called Abigaelle because she had finished the tutorial weeks ago and because she enjoyed being right in a way that was mostly survivable. She came over with her laptop and a bag of chips she did not share, and stood over his shoulder while he complained. "The zone says these houses aren't at risk," he said. "But look where they are."

"So define near," she said, mouth full.

"That's the thing. How do I even, in the software, draw near. Not by hand. There are three hundred houses."

Abigaelle set down the chips, which was how he knew the answer mattered. "You make a buffer," she said. "A buffer draws a zone of a set distance around a feature. Every area within a hundred meters of the river, if that's the distance you pick."

He stared at her. "That's it? That's a thing it just does?"

"That's a thing it just does. You're welcome. Also that's my chip."

He built the buffer at a hundred meters, ran it around the river's whole length, and overlaid the housing layer on top. The map bloomed with a soft gray band hugging every bend, and where the band crossed Sycamore Street the parcels inside it turned a color he had chosen without thinking and then had to sit with: a vivid, accusatory orange. He began to collate the addresses, matching parcel numbers to the tax records the county site let him download after three misleading menus. It was slow, careful work, and he liked it more than he expected to, the way the mess of pixels resolved into an argument.

Then he typed his own address, half to test the lookup and half out of the idle vanity of seeing home rendered as data, and the parcel turned orange.

He sat back. His house was on Sycamore. Outside the official flood zone, no disclosure had ever mentioned water, his mother had once said the basement flooded "once, years ago, it was a whole thing," and now here was the house, orange, inside the band of a hundred meters, a fact he had generated himself on a Tuesday with a bag of chips on the table. The mercurial river two blocks away, which he had regarded his whole life as scenery, was suddenly a variable.

"Benjamin?" His mother was at the counter, unloading a bag of groceries with the deliberate calm she used when she suspected something. "Is something wrong?"

"Class project," he said. "Flood risk and housing."

"Mm. Anything interesting?"

He looked at the screen, at the orange rectangle that was the roof over their kitchen. He could show her. He could explain the buffer, the distance, the way the official zone stopped short of their street, and watch her decide whether to worry. Or he could close the laptop and let the information be his for one more night, one more week, until he understood what it was worth.

"Depends what you mean by interesting," he said.

His mother set a jar on the counter and looked at him for a moment longer than the sentence required. "Dinner's at seven," she said, and turned back to the groceries. Abigaelle, watching all of this over a chip, raised one eyebrow at him and said nothing.

He turned back to the map and made the orange a quieter color, a shade closer to the others, though he left it on. Then he opened the county's data page again and started a new column, titled it, and typed his own address in the first row.

"Number two," Abigaelle said, reading upside down. "What's number one?"

"Sycamore, four-oh-nine," he said. "The Amiras. Their yard is lower than ours."

activity: going on a first date
story:
Eva had read the paragraph twice on the bus, once in Lyla's kitchen, and a third time in the parking lot of the bowling alley before she pocketed her phone like evidence. "In 1999," Lyla had told her, scrolling through her psych notes, "Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry." Lyla had looked up with the particular grin of someone handing over a loaded gift. "So if you want him to like you, copy him."

The automatic doors parted with a sigh, and Eva stepped into the blue-white glow of Fairlanes, where the carpet had gone bald in lanes of its own and the smell of fryer oil felt autochthonous, as native to the place as the scoring screens flickering overhead. Khalid was already at the counter, juggling two pairs of shoes, and when he turned and saw her he did a small silent bow, like a waiter presenting a wine list. She laughed before she had decided to.

They ended up with lane eleven, which Khalid declared lucky because eleven looked like two people standing side by side, or one person who had brought a friend. He entered their names as EVA and KOHLRABI, which she made him fix, and then the fixing took three tries because he kept typing his own name wrong on purpose. She found she liked watching him be ridiculous. She found she was also cataloguing him, and she disliked that part, the little clipboard in her head ticking off items: polite to the cashier, good laugh, terrible shoes.

In the third frame she noticed the elbows. She had leaned onto the scoring table, chin in her palm, and when she glanced over, Khalid was leaning on the same table, chin in his palm, the same tilt, the same slack wrist. She felt a small electric embarrassment, as though she'd caught him reading her diary, and then a worse thought: what if he had read the same thing she had. Everyone in their grade took the same elective. She straightened up quickly, as if the table had gone hot.

"So my friend Lyla thinks first dates are, like, a liminality thing," she said, mostly to fill the air she'd just vacated. "You're between being strangers and being whatever you are after. No rules in either direction yet." Khalid considered this while weighing a ball, and then bowled a strike, all wrist and follow-through, and turned back to her with his eyes narrowed. "That's actually good. My grandmother would say you're at a door that hasn't decided which room it is yet." He said it kindly, and she found herself leaning forward again without meaning to, and found him already leaning.

Her next ball went straight into the gutter, both throws, and she bowed to the empty lane. "I would like to expiate that," she announced, "but I don't know what bowling requires. A sacrifice of nachos, maybe." He laughed too loudly, and then, mid-laugh, she saw it happen in reverse: she had her hand flat on the table, and he put his hand flat on the table. Not looking at her. Not looking at his hand either, which was somehow the eerie part. She thought about Chartrand and Bargh again, about how in 1999 they had found that people liked a partner more when that partner mimicked their posture and gestures, and how the strange thing, the thing Lyla had underlined twice, was that nobody noticed the mimicry happening. Well. Almost nobody.

She tried an experiment, the kind she'd have mocked Lyla for designing. On her next turn she crossed her ankles and stood with her weight on her back foot, hands jammed in her pockets. When she came back from the lane with a respectable eight pins, Khalid was standing with his weight on his back foot, hands jammed in his pockets. She watched his face for the effort of it, for the flicker of calculation, and found nothing, only that he was asking whether she wanted a soda, and by the time she'd said yes they were both walking to the counter in step, left foot and left foot, like a couple in a movie neither of them had auditioned for.

Then she caught herself doing it back. He scratched the back of his neck reading the menu, and ten seconds later her own hand drifted up, and she stood there with her fingers on her collar and a cold, clarifying feeling. It didn't matter who had started it. She could not tell, from the inside, whether she was copying him because she liked him, or liking him because she was copying him, and there was no lane of her mind where those two things rolled separately. Lyla's fact was still true, she was sure, still exactly as true as 1999 had made it, and it told her nothing about which one of them was the author.

He came back with two sodas and a plate of nachos he swore were for expiation purposes only, and they ate them at the little table behind the lanes, and he told her about his grandmother's door theory and she told him about Lyla's psych notes, and she stopped just short of the study itself, holding it behind her teeth like a coin. Some things you spend, she thought, and some things you keep to see if they were real.

By the tenth frame she had stopped keeping score, which the scoreboard did anyway, flashing its indifferent arithmetic above them. Khalid bowled, and she watched him, and she made no decision about her posture at all, letting it do whatever it was going to do. When he rolled a strike he turned around with both arms up, and she realized hers were up too, and neither of them said anything about it.

"Same time next week?" he asked, sliding the shoes off with his heel.

"Ask me at the door," she said. "The one that hasn't decided which room it is yet."

story:
The first practice of the season, Autumn counted fifteen girls standing in a loose ring on the alluvial flat behind the school, the field the river had left behind after some ancient flood, dark soil that took cleats like a gift. Nobody knew where to stand. Rosemarie asked her name twice. Sidney, who had played club for years, held the ball under her arm like she owned it, and everyone let her, because it was easier to follow than to decide. They lost their first three games without arguing once, which Autumn later understood was its own kind of problem.

The fighting began in October, on a Tuesday, over a throw-in nobody would remember by Friday. Sidney called Rosemarie slow getting back on defense. Rosemarie said Sidney hogged the ball, and imputed worse to her besides, a selfishness that had nothing to do with the play, that she'd apparently been saving up since September. Two other girls took sides. The coach sent them all on laps, and during the laps nobody ran together, each girl tracing her own private oval of fury across the grass.

That evening Ms. Fortin, who taught psychology two doors down from Autumn's last class, was collecting cones from the adjacent field. Autumn had stayed to collect her own thoughts, or at least her shin guards, which had scattered under the bench. "You look like a team that just discovered it has opinions," Ms. Fortin said, stacking the cones. Then, quieter, almost offhand: "Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages. Forming, storming, norming, performing." She hefted the cones onto her hip. "You're in the second one, I'd guess." She walked off toward the parking lot before Autumn could ask what came after.

Autumn looked it up that night anyway, at the kitchen table while her mother washed dishes. Four stages, in order, like rungs. What stayed unclear was whether knowing the ladder helped you climb it, or only let you name the height you fell from. She copied the words into the back of her planner and then felt slightly ridiculous, a midfielder with a theory.

She didn't tell the others right away. But at Thursday's practice, when Sidney and Rosemarie started again, this time over who should take a free kick, Autumn stepped between them at the top of the box. "We're storming," she said. Both of them stared. "It's a thing. It means we're actually becoming a team, the fighting part. It's supposed to come before the good part." Sidney's mouth twitched toward a smirk and then, unexpectedly, stopped halfway. "That's the most annoying thing anyone's ever said to me," she said, "and I can't tell if it's comforting." Rosemarie laughed for the first time in a week.

The norms came slowly and without ceremony. Rosemarie started calling "ball" louder, so Sidney could hear her. Sidney started laying passes off instead of driving alone into three defenders. In the last game of the regular season they pressed a better team for eighty minutes, and when the final whistle came, they had lost by one goal and were grinning anyway, hooked arm in arm near the center circle, exhausted in a way that felt shared. Autumn felt something in her chest that she didn't have a name for, and didn't trust herself to name it.

The season ended in the first round of playoffs, on a cold Saturday, on a penalty kick that Rosemarie took and the keeper saved. Driving home, her father tried to console her by calling the season a success anyway, development, experience, all the words adults reach for, and Autumn said yes, sure, while knowing it was only half true. A theory that fit the team's life so neatly felt like a kind of indemnity, a contract against future disappointment, except that it paid out nothing when Rosemarie stood at the spot with the whole game in her foot and missed. Knowing the stages didn't save you from them. Maybe all it did was let you stand in the storm and believe it would pass, which was not nothing, and also not enough.

In spring, the rec league put out flyers, and Rosemarie texted her a photo of one, followed by a question mark. Autumn sat on her bed looking at it for a long time. Then she pulled her cleats from the closet, still caked in river-dark soil from the field behind the school, and began picking the dried crumbs of it out of the studs with her thumbnail.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Autumn spread the papers across the kitchen table the way her mother used to lay out a jigsaw, edges first, sky last. Her father's tax return was due tomorrow at midnight, and he was on nights at the plant, sleeping in the bedroom with the door shut, so the whole thing had landed on her: the T4 slip in its blue header, the receipts rubber-banded in an envelope, the online account whose password he had written on a napkin and then eaten half of. The overhead light buzzed. She could smell the dish soap still drying on the counter and, faintly, coffee gone cold in the pot.

Her paycheque stub from the bakery lay under her elbow where she'd left it, and she kept drifting to it instead of her father's forms. Six weeks of Saturday shifts, and her first cheque had been smaller than the number she'd been promised. She had done the arithmetic three times that evening: $412 gross, then a column of deductions, federal and provincial, CPP, EI, each line a small subtraction she hadn't agreed to but had somehow consented to anyway, until the net pay sat at the bottom like a stone at the bottom of a stream. $369.41.

Hiba arrived at nine with her bank app already open, holding her phone out before her coat was off. "Guess what. Guess. My dad's refund came through today. Fourteen hundred dollars. He's taking us for dinner Friday, actual dinner, not drive-through." She dropped into the chair across from Autumn and slid the phone across the table so the green deposit line faced her like proof. "Free money, basically. Like the government just gives it to you in the spring if you filed."

Rogan, who had come for the chemistry homework and stayed for the forms because he claimed he was a connoisseur of other people's paperwork disasters, leaned over the table and read the screen upside down. "Free," he repeated, in the flat, sardonic way he said words he didn't buy. "Nothing about the government is free. They sent my dad a bill in April once. I thought he was going to move us to the woods."

"It's not the same thing," Hiba said. "A bill means you owe. A refund means they owe you. It goes in, not out. Look at the little arrow."

Autumn looked. The green line, the plus sign, the date. She was glad for Hiba, whose father worked double shifts at the warehouse and who had been wearing the same winter coat since grade nine, and Friday dinners mattered in that house the way they didn't in others. But something about the shape of it bothered her, a loose thread. She pulled her father's return folder toward her and found the page from last year, the assessment summary, and set it beside her own paycheque stub. Two documents, two years, one table under one buzzing light.

"Wait," she said slowly, running her finger down the stub's deduction column. "They take it off every pay. Off mine, off your dad's, off everyone's, the whole year, before it even reaches us. So the money was his the whole time." She looked up. "It's not extra income. It's an overpayment. If he got a refund, it means they withheld more during the year than he actually owed, and they're giving back the difference. It was his fourteen hundred dollars in January."

Hiba's face did something complicated, the celebration destabilizing for a second before she caught it. "But it still arrives in April. It still feels like spring money. He still budgets for it like it's a gift." She said it almost defensively, and then, quieter: "He calls it his bonus."

"I'm not saying don't have dinner," Autumn said. "I'm saying it's his own money coming home late." Rogan snorted at that, but not unkindly; he reached across and squared the crooked stack of receipts, aligning their edges, which was the closest he came to tenderness.

At ten thirty the doorbell rang, and it was Mr. Qureshi from two doors down, holding a plate of his wife's baklava and asking, in his apologetic way, whether their water had gone brown too, because his had, and he wanted to know if he should call the city before morning. Autumn took the plate, said yes, brown, and got him a glass from the filtered pitcher without being asked. He peered at the table on his way out and said only, "Deadline tomorrow?" and she nodded, and he said, "Your mother did mine the year she was here," and went home, and Autumn stood in the doorway a moment longer than she needed to, holding the plate, smelling honey and pistachio and the cold off his coat.

She filed it at 11:52, her father's signature obtained in pencil-drowsy confusion over the phone, and when the confirmation screen came up she took a photograph of it with her phone in case the internet, or the government, or the world tried to take it back. Then she sat looking at the bakery stub again. She would file her own tiny return in a few weeks, and somewhere in the machinery of the year a small amount of her Saturday mornings was sitting, waiting, already hers, already owed back. Whether it would come back as a refund or a bill, she couldn't yet say; the arithmetic of a whole year was longer than any evening.

"Next April," Hiba said, pulling on her coat, "when my dad gets his refund, I'm going to tell him it's just his January money coming home. And then I'm still going to eat the dinner."

"Both of those," Rogan said, "are the correct position."

Autumn laughed, and folded the paycheque stub into her back pocket, where she'd feel it against the chair all through tomorrow's shift.

story:
Connor had drawn the drill on graph paper the night before, three cones and a dashed line meant to cure the eleven-year-olds of throwing to nobody. The backyard was his only field: his father had strung a net between the fence and the garage years ago, back when Connor was the one being coached, and the grass there still showed the bald rectangle where feet had worn it. Now Rex sat on the porch steps with the paper while Connor dragged cones into the same tired pattern.

"Okay," Rex said, reading. "One kid runs the line, the other passes. If the ball's late, you tell him what he did wrong. Bend the wrist, step into it, follow through."

"That's the whole point of a drill," Connor said. "You isolate the mistake and you fix it."

Rex folded the paper in half, which felt to Connor like a small indictment of hours of planning, though Rex probably only meant to keep the wind from taking it. "Did it ever work on you?" Rex asked. "When Harris's dad used to yell pointers at us from the sideline?"

Connor remembered standing at a free throw line at fourteen, every shot dissolving the moment somebody shouted "elbow in." He remembered the net himself, the summer it went up, learning passes against it alone because nobody his age would practice something so basic. He said, "Mostly it made me think about my elbow."

They ran the drill anyway on Saturday with six kids from the younger team, the net sagging overhead like something pelagic, a deep blue tarp his mother had repurposed, billowing. The results were the same as last week's game: passes sailing wide, receivers stopping to watch the ball instead of running to it. Connor corrected. Bend your wrist. Turn your hips. Point your foot at the target. The kids nodded and got worse, their arms stiff with self-consciousness, and by the end even he could see they were thinking about their bodies instead of the play.

Ms. Augustin, the neighbour whose garden butted against their fence, had been listening over the beans while she watered. She was retired from teaching something at the college and had opinions she mostly kept to herself. That evening she set a book on the porch rail, a paperback about how people learn movement, and said only, "The chapter on attention is the interesting one. It catalyzed some arguments in my old department." Then she went back inside, which was her way.

Connor read it that night, sprawled on the garage roof below his bedroom window. Gabriele Wulf had done research and found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts. He read it twice. He thought about his elbow, his free throws, the kids' rigid arms. It was the opposite of everything he had planned for, the whole method of the drill, and it refused to resolve into something comfortable. He had spent two evenings designing corrections that were, quite possibly, the problem.

On Sunday he ran the same drill with the same cones and said nothing about wrists, hips, or feet. "Hit Rex in the hands," he told the first kid. "Put the ball where his hands are going to be." The pass was ugly, the footwork unorthodox, and it arrived anyway. The second kid grinned and called for it. By the third round they were moving without being told, chasing the ball to the spot instead of waiting for it to find them, and Harris, who had come over to watch and had started out mocking the cones, was holding up his palms as a target without anyone asking him.

"Where'd you get that?" Harris asked afterward, nodding at the paperback on the steps. "The hands thing."

"Ms. Augustin. Wulf found people learn faster focusing on the target, not their body parts," Connor said. "I got it backwards for a week."

It was not that clean, and he knew it. One kid, the smallest, still threw flat-footed no matter what Connor said, and maybe a drill about planting and pivoting would fix that, or maybe it would wreck what was working. He didn't know yet where the line was between a body that needed correcting and a target that needed naming, and the book hadn't drawn one either. He gathered the cones as the light went. Rex held the tarp net while Connor untied the last corner, and the blue fabric came down over them both like a wave, and from under it Rex said, "Same time Tuesday. Tell them to hit my hands, not my face."

story:
Lucas had forty minutes to fix a painting that had gone wrong in the second layer and kept going wronger since. The assignment was a portrait of someone you knew, and he had chosen his grandmother, who had died in March, and now her face sat on the easel looking like it had been sunburned by a radiator. Ms. Siddiqui came down the row of tables, stopped behind him, and said nothing, which was worse than criticism because it left him to supply it himself.

"It's the colors," he said finally. "I don't know what to put against the orange so it stops screaming."

"Complementary," said Eamon from the next table without looking up from his collage. "Orange and blue. Even I know that, and I'm failing this class."

Lucas had heard the word before, in the rushed September unit on color theory, but hearing it now felt different, like a tool he actually needed. He turned to the shelf by the window where Ms. Siddiqui kept her battered reference books and pulled out a thin one with a cracked spine, older than any textbook the school had issued him. Inside were hand-drawn circles of color, red flowing into yellow into green into blue, the whole rainbow bent around a ring.

He carried it back to his table and opened it beside his palette. Dean leaned over from across the aisle, chewing the end of a brush. "That's a physics book," Dean said. "Why is there a physics book in the art room?"

Lucas looked at the title page. Opticks. He turned further in, past diagrams of prisms and beams, and found the circle again, printed small and careful. The caption gave a date, 1704, and a name he knew from a science class he'd barely survived: Isaac Newton.

"Newton made this," Lucas said. "The color wheel. It was Newton." He said it quietly, the way you might report a piece of gossip you weren't sure you believed. "A physicist arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, in his 1704 book, and it became the thing artists use."

Dean squinted at the page. "So when Eamon said orange and blue, that was basically Newton talking."

"Eamon would love to hear that," Lucas said.

Eamon, hearing it, spread his arms as if accepting an award. Ms. Siddiqui passed behind them again and paused just long enough to look at the open book, the painting, and Lucas's face, in that order. "Now you have a reason to trust the wheel," she said, and moved on, and Lucas understood that this was the entire lecture she intended to give.

He mixed a blue, thinned it, and laid it into the background behind his grandmother's left shoulder. The effect was immediate and strange. The orange of her face didn't disappear; it found a counterpoint, a tension that held the two colors in place like two people leaning against each other. He had wanted the problem solved, but this wasn't solved, exactly. It was balanced, which was not the same thing, and he could feel the difference without being able to verbalize it, though he tried, muttering "it's not quieter, it's more" before giving up on sentences.

What he could not fix was the likeness. He had thought the colors were the whole trouble, and for an hour that had been a comforting belief, because colors were technical and technique could be learned. But the mouth was wrong in a way no wheel would correct. His grandmother had smiled with one side of her mouth first, a half-second before the other side joined, and no single painted expression could hold that sequence, that delay, that person. He kept painting anyway, because stopping felt like a decision and painting was only a continuation.

Dean drifted over during cleanup, looked at the portrait for a long moment, and said, "It doesn't look like a photo of her."

"No," Lucas said.

"But it looks like remembering her," Dean said, and then, seeming embarrassed by his own sentence, busied himself stacking jars of brushes with unnecessary force.

Eamon's voice carried from the sink, something tangential about whether Newton had also invented the seesaw, and whether physicists owed artists an apology or a thank-you card. Lucas didn't answer. He was looking at the small circle in the old book, the spectrum curled shut, red touching its own beginning again. A physicist he'd never understood had reached across three hundred years to hand him this ring, and it had helped with exactly the part of the painting that mattered least. The part that mattered most was still his alone, still unfinished, still one-sided in its smile.

He wiped his brush on a rag and stayed after the bell, adding a thin line of blue beneath her jaw, then another, the room emptying around him.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
story:
The granite soldier at the county war memorial had a crack running down his rifle arm, and Anais had chosen him anyway, because the light at four o'clock hit his face in a way that looked less like bronze heroism and more like a boy squinting against wind. She crouched on the steps with her phone, re-recording the opening line of her video essay for the third time, while Konnor held the reflector he had made out of cardboard and foil and complained that his arms were tired.

"From the top," she said. "And this time don't sneeze."

"I didn't sneeze, I breathed. There's a difference."

Cheyanne sat cross-legged on the plinth, out of frame, reading aloud from her own screen. "Pericles' Funeral Oration. 'Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a minority but of the whole people.'" She looked up. "That's your quote, right? The one you're opening with?"

Anais hit record. The assignment was Mr. Nolan's: connect an ancient primary source to something standing in their own town, and argue the connection. She had spent two nights on it, and she had a thesis she liked, that the memorial and the oration were both performances of grief shaped into civic instruction, grief made useful. She said a version of this into the phone, then climbed the steps and laid her palm flat on the cold base, because the essay needed a closing image and she thought she had found one.

Afterward, sorting clips in the shade of the monument's one elm, Konnor scrolling with his thumb, Cheyanne said, "You know those aren't his actual words. Pericles' words."

"What?"

"Thucydides. The guy who wrote it down." Cheyanne turned her phone so Anais could see the passage, and Mr. Nolan, who had been across the lawn talking to a groundskeeper, wandered over in time to hear the next sentence. "He admits the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War weren't word-for-word records. He wrote what he judged each speaker would have needed to say."

Anais took the phone. She read the translator's note twice. "So I've been standing here quoting a reconstruction."

"A good one," Konnor offered, sardonic as always when he thought someone was taking themselves too seriously. "Two thousand years of people quoting it can't all be wrong."

"That's not how that works," Anais said, but without heat, because the ground was shifting under her in a way she found she wanted to examine rather than defend against. She sat down on the step beside Cheyanne. If the words were partly Thucydides' invention, then her whole essay was quoting a ghost wearing Pericles' face, and the ghost was a general who had fought in the war he was describing, writing decades later from memory and judgment. She thought about the plaque on the memorial's back side, which she had read in September: one hundred and eleven names, and under them a line about dying so that others might be free. Her grandfather had once called that phrase emancipation-talk, the town's polite way of folding every death into one tidy purpose, and her mother had called the same phrase, when she was feeling bitter, a dysphemism dressed as praise, a way of making the dying sound like they had chosen it. Same words. Two listeners. She had never known which of them to agree with, and had mostly chosen neither.

"It's not ruined," Cheyanne said quietly, watching her face. "It might be better."

Mr. Nolan, who had been no help at all, in the way he seemed to think was help, had drifted back toward the parking lot. Konnor handed Anais the last of the water and didn't say anything clever, which she noticed and appreciated.

She walked back up the steps and stood in front of the cracked soldier. The truth was that Thucydides had told them, up front, that he was making something, and that telling them was itself a kind of honesty; the town's plaque had made no such confession. Maybe that was the real comparison, not the monuments' shared grief but their different relationship to what could be known. She wasn't sure. She was sure of the cold under her hand, and of Cheyanne waiting, and of the fact that the light had moved and she would have to shoot the ending again from a different angle.

"Konnor," she said, "hold the reflector a little more left. And Cheyanne, when I finish, read me that translator's note on camera. I want it in the video, right after I say the quote, so nobody watches it the way I watched it an hour ago."

"Anais quoting Pericles quoting nobody," Konnor said, lifting the foil.

"Thucydides," she said, and hit record.
