activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
The gym smelled like hot glue and anxiety, and Austin had forty minutes before the judges made their rounds. His poster read "Salt Saturation at Room Temperature" in letters he had redone twice, and his data table had a hole in it the shape of a single missing number. He knew the mass of his salt bag, 175.32 grams, because he had weighed it three times on the kitchen scale while his mother asked whether the scale was food-safe. What he did not know, and what Ms. González would absolutely ask about, was how many moles of sodium chloride that actually was.

"Stop vibrating," said Cassandre, adjusting her own poster about moss growth on different roofs. "You're making the table shake. My moss can feel it."

"My moss data has a mole-sized gap," Austin said. "The whole back half of my results depends on it. I solved for concentration in moles, and I never converted the bag."

Cassandre peered at his notebook, where he had written 175.32 and then, in increasingly desperate handwriting, nothing. "So convert it now. You have the periodic table right there."

He did have it, taped to the corner of the poster like a decorative flourish. The problem was that a periodic table told you what sodium weighed and what chlorine weighed, and somewhere between those two facts and his bag of table salt, arithmetic kept going sideways in his head. He tried 22.99 plus 35.45, got 58.44, and then sat very still.

"That's the molar mass," he said aloud. "Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole. One mole of salt weighs fifty-eight point four four grams."

"Congratulations," said Cassandre. "Would you like a plaque, or is the poster enough?"

From two tables down, Kailyn leaned over her elaborate setup, a ramp, a toy car, and a sign promising "Friction: The Silent Thief." Kailyn's project had placed second at regionals last year, and she had announced at 7:40 that morning that anything less than first this year was, in her words, a personal insult. She wanted the trophy the way other people wanted water. "González always asks the mole question," she called over. "Every year. She asked me about moles when I did friction. Friction, Austin. There were no moles involved."

"That's exactly my fear," Austin said.

He set up the division on the back of Cassandre's moss handout, since it was the only clean paper within reach and she made a noise of protest he ignored. 175.32 divided by 58.44. He worked it through, carrying digits, redoing the carry when his handwriting betrayed him, and got approximately three. Three moles in the bag. He checked it the only way he could think of, by multiplying back: three times 58.44 was 175.32. The numbers closed on each other like a zipper, and he felt something loosen in his chest that had been tight since breakfast.

"So your saturation point," Cassandre said, reading over his shoulder, "per liter, per mole, the whole thing?"

"Per liter. Which means I can finally finish the table." He wrote the last row of numbers in pen, which felt reckless and wonderful, like signing a contract in blood.

Ms. González arrived at 9:12 with a clipboard and the pleasant, unhurried manner of someone about to dismantle a teenager's morning. She did not expatiate on the virtues of quantitative rigor, though Austin sensed she could have, at length. Instead she picked up the salt bag, turned it over, and said, "Walk me through your numbers."

He walked her through them. The mass, the molar mass, the division, the multiplication that checked it. She asked what would change if the bag had been a hundred grams, and he said out loud, before fully deciding to, "Fewer moles, but the same saturation concentration, because saturation is about the water, not the bag." Ms. González wrote something on her clipboard, and Austin could not tell whether it was approval or the beginning of a follow-up question designed to ruin him. He was honest with himself about that, at least. He did not know.

She moved on to Kailyn's ramp, where the toy car had, in the interim, rolled off the table and wedged itself under the bleachers. Kailyn knelt on the floor retrieving it, muttering something vitriolic about gravity, which Cassandre later pointed out was a strange thing for a friction researcher to resent.

"You realize," Cassandre said, snapping a photo of Austin's finished table for posterity, "that 'calm chemist' is basically an oxymoron."

"It's not calm," Austin said. "It's three moles of composure, roughly, per poster." He was still unsure the concentration joke made sense, and he said it anyway, and Kailyn, from under the bleachers, shouted, "I can hear you, and it's terrible."

Austin straightened his poster, set the salt bag front and center like a witness, and watched the next judge cross the gym floor toward him.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
Isabella had not left her research paper until the last weekend possible, a fact she repeated to herself on the train out to her grandmother's house, where she planned to finish it in two days of focused, almost ascetic concentration. The kitchen table had been cleared of the puzzle magazines and the tin of ginger biscuits her grandmother pretended not to keep. Her laptop was open. Her sources were in a folder. It was, by any reasonable account, an ideal setup, and Isabella was the kind of person who did well with ideal setups.

The paper was about the Dutch purchase of Manhattan, and her thesis, which she had written first because Ms. Hoang said a paper without an argument was just a tour, was that the famous twenty-four-dollar price tag was less a swindle than a misunderstanding about what either party thought they were selling. She had a book from the library, three articles printed at school, and a museum website. She had been told to use footnotes and a bibliography in Chicago style, which she had chosen herself out of stubbornness, and which she now regretted at intervals of roughly nine minutes.

Her grandmother drifted through the kitchen making tea and offering commentary. "Twenty-four dollars," she said, reading over Isabella's shoulder. "For an island. Your grandfather once paid six for a parking spot in the city, and he still tells it like a victory."

"It wasn't dollars exactly," Isabella said. "That's the conversion part. It was trade goods." She typed the sentence she was most pleased with: The transaction reveals less about greed than about two groups operating with entirely different notions of ownership. It sounded like her, she decided. It sounded like the kind of thing a person would underline.

The trouble, if it could be called trouble, and Isabella initially called it efficiency, was the library book. The historian's chapter said the sale hinged on incompatible ideas of land as property versus land as shared resource, and Isabella had put the book's paragraph into her own words so thoroughly, so completely rephrased, that it seemed obvious the ideas were now hers. She had transformed the sentences; the sentences had surrendered. There was no copying when nothing matched. She wrote the footnote for the two places where she'd kept the historian's actual phrasing and moved on, feeling rather brilliant about the whole business.

On Sunday morning she was on her second page of the bibliography when Genevieve texted a photo of her own draft, captioned "how many footnotes is too many footnotes," and Cordelia replied in the group chat, "for Hoang? there is no too many, she put a comment on mine that said 'nice paraphrase, where's the citation.'" Isabella read that message twice. She set the phone face down, picked it up, read it again, and then opened her paper and looked at her transformed paragraph, which had suddenly stopped looking like a transformation and started looking like something she had taken without asking.

She went into the garden where her grandmother was deadheading the roses and stated, with the flat confidence of a person testing a theory aloud, "If you put someone's idea in your own words, you still have to cite it. Plagiarism isn't just copying the exact words. It's using ideas without credit." Her grandmother snipped a spent bloom and said, "That sounds right. That also sounds like something you already knew."

"That's a truism," Isabella said, mostly to buy time. "Everyone says it."

"Everyone says it because it's true," her grandmother said. "Also, you told me Friday you'd invented your whole argument in the shower."

Isabella recalibrated. Not the argument, exactly, and not the thesis, which she had honestly assembled from three sources disagreeing with each other, but the middle section, the part she'd been proudest of, which turned out to be a borrowed insight wearing her clothes. She went back inside, added the footnote, numbered it properly, rebuilt the bibliography entry from the front of the book, and then, because honesty once started is apparently difficult to stop, went through the entire paper and found two more places where she'd absorbed someone's framing so completely she'd forgotten it had an author. One was the museum website. One was, embarrassingly, a line Genevieve had said out loud in the library two weeks ago, which no citation style had a format for, so she just changed it.

She sent the draft to Ms. Hoang that night, before she could reconsider. The reply came Monday morning, one line: "This is much better than what you described to me on Thursday, when you said it was basically done." Isabella read it in the train station, holding her phone with both hands.

She had, in fact, told Ms. Hoang on Thursday that the paper was basically done. She had also told Genevieve she didn't need the weekend. She had told herself, all week, that she was the sort of person who finished things early. Her grandmother, presumably, had known otherwise since Friday, and had cleared the table anyway, and had kept the biscuits coming without comment.

Genevieve texted again: "footnote count final?" Isabella typed "31," deleted it, typed the real number, which was 14, and sent that instead.

"Respect," Cordelia wrote. "Hoang's going to think you learned something."

Isabella looked out the train window at the river going by, gray and indifferent, and put the phone in her pocket, unfinished.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
The basket handle bit into Justin's palm by the time he reached the dairy aisle. His mother's text had come during fourth period: double shift, fridge is a crime scene, please make dinner, eggs on the second shelf, love you. He had read it eleven times, the way you reread a verdict. Eighteen years old and he had never cooked anything that did not involve a microwave, and now his father and his little sister were going to sit at a table at seven o'clock and look at him.

"Mayonnaise from scratch," Brent said, trailing behind him with a bag of chips he had no intention of paying for, only carrying. "Who are you, a factory?"

"Mr. Rossi said his mother made it by hand every Friday. He said it takes ten minutes."

"Mr. Rossi also thinks the school board is a plutocracy."

"He's not wrong." Justin picked up a carton of eggs, checked each one for cracks, put it back, chose another. The recipe on his phone was from some site with a watermark, four ingredients, one bowl, a whisk. Oil, egg yolk, lemon, salt. How hard could suspension be. He took two lemons he did not need, in case of failure, and a jar of the store brand, in case of worse failure.

At the register, Eden was working the till, her hair pinned up with a pencil. She scanned the oil slowly, turning the bottle to read the label like it had insulted her. "You know this is the wrong oil for mayonnaise," she said. "It'll taste like crayons."

"It says neutral oil."

"It says that on the crayons too." She demurred when he asked her to just scan it, held the bottle a moment longer, then let it go. "If it splits," she said, "don't throw it out. My grandmother fixed one once with a raw yolk. I was six and I thought it was magic." Justin paid, took his bags, and told her he would text her a photo of the finished jar, which he already suspected was a promise made to a future liar.

In the kitchen the first three minutes went well. Yolk in the bowl, whisk, salt, a squeeze of lemon. Then the oil, drop by drop, which the recipe insisted on, and which he obeyed for approximately eleven drops before ambition took over and he poured. The mixture went glossy, then strange, then it broke apart in front of him, a yellow puddle swimming in a lake of oil, and no amount of whisking called it back together. His sister stood in the doorway eating a string cheese and narrating. "It looks like a science accident," she said. "I'm telling Dad it's a science accident."

He texted Brent first, because texting his mother would mean admitting the evening was in danger. Brent replied in fragments: "did u add the oil slow," "u didn't," "u absolute spoon." Then Brent sent a photo of a takeout menu with the caption "the plutocracy of victory," which was not funny, and then, a minute later, "ask Rossi. he literally talks about mayo like it's family." Justin looked at the broken bowl, at the clock, at his sister, who had begun drumming the table.

Here is what I understood, standing in Mr. Rossi's doorway with the whole bowl carried over like an offering: nothing. I knew the yolk had something in it, because Eden had said so, and because my grandmother had said so before her, though I had been too young to listen. Mr. Rossi put on his glasses, looked into the bowl, and did not laugh, which was its own kind of mercy.

"Your emulsion broke," he said. "Happens to everyone once."

"Is that what those are called? Emulsions?"

"The yolk makes it one. The lecithin and the proteins in it, they're emulsifiers. They hold the oil in tiny droplets, suspended in the water, so the sauce doesn't separate." He said it the way he said everything, flat, like a man reading a shipping label, and went to his fridge for another egg without ceremony.

He separated the yolk into a clean bowl, and then he made me do the rest. Drop of oil, whisk. Drop, whisk. He would not touch the whisk. My arm burned and my sister, who had followed me across the hall in her socks, kept asking if we were poor now. Then the new yolk pulled the old wreckage in, spoonful by spoonful, the split mess from my bowl folding into this fresh gold and thickening, holding, becoming one thing. When it was done it stood up on the whisk in a slow ribbon, and Mr. Rossi said, "There," and nothing else.

I carried it home and made the rest of dinner, which was just chicken and bread, honestly, the mayonnaise carrying the whole meal on its back. My father asked twice whether it was store-bought, and my sister, who had watched the rescue from a kitchen that was not ours, kept saying "it's a science accident" in a tone that made my father laugh into his plate. I texted Eden the photo after the dishes. She replied with a single thumbs up, and then, a minute later: "told you. yolk = magic." I typed out that it wasn't magic, that it was lecithin and proteins holding tiny oil droplets in the water, then deleted it, because she already knew, and because part of me wanted to keep it magic anyway.

My mother came home at ten, ate cold chicken standing at the counter, and licked the spoon twice before she said anything. "You made this," she said, and it wasn't a question, and she took the jar out of the fridge and turned it in the light, watching the slow, held shine of it tilt.

story:
The recliner in Grandpa's basement had a permanent dent shaped like him, and Elijah had claimed it an hour before tipoff, which meant everyone arriving late treated him as furniture. Hayden dropped onto the armrest without asking, and Kolton sprawled on the carpet with his phone face-up, already narrating the game to people who were also watching the game. Above them, through the ceiling, the cousins and uncles crowded the better television, and their roars arrived a half second early, like thunder before you find the lightning.

"Marlowe's got twenty-eight in the third quarter," Kolton said. "He's on fire. Nobody's stopping him tonight."

"I don't know," Hayden said, chewing a pretzel slowly, which was how he signaled an opinion was coming. "Streaks aren't real. You make a few and everyone starts believing in you. It's in your head."

Elijah had spent the drive to Grandpa's reading about exactly this, and the timing felt almost staged. "There's an actual study," he said, and immediately regretted the tone, which sounded like a teacher's. He tried again, quieter. "In 1985, three researchers, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, looked at thousands of shots and said the hot hand doesn't exist. They called it an illusion."

Kolton sat up. "Called what an illusion?"

"The hot hand. That's the phrase in the paper. The idea that a player who's hit a few in a row is more likely to hit the next one. They said no, the makes and misses are basically random, and fans just see patterns."

He had found it three weeks ago, and the memory returned to him now with the smell of Grandpa's basement, coffee and cedar. It had been two in the morning, the summer before everything, and he had gone looking for a way to win an argument with his uncle about playoff basketball and instead found a fight between strangers that had lasted thirty years. He'd read the 1985 paper in one sitting, feeling the satisfaction of a door closing: streaks were superstition, grown men in rep ties believing in magic. Then, scrolling, he'd found the other one.

On screen Marlowe rose over two defenders and made it anyway, and the ceiling thundered. Mr. Hussain, Grandpa's neighbor of thirty years, came down the stairs carrying his own mug, because in this house that was how consanguinity worked even without blood; he had a chair here the way he had a chair in his own kitchen. He settled into it and said, "That boy is not missing tonight. Some nights the rim just looks bigger."

"That's what everybody thought," Elijah said. "But here's the thing. In 2018, two guys, Miller and Sanjurjo, went back and reanalyzed it, and they found a flaw in the statistics. Some kind of error in the way the original study did its math. And when they fixed it, they found evidence of streak shooting after all. That a player who's made his last few actually does have a better chance on the next one."

"So they were both right?" Hayden asked.

"So they were both wrong first," Kolton said, grinning.

Elijah laughed, but the question stayed with him, working at him the way a loose tooth works at you. Because which one was he supposed to believe now? The clean story was the 1985 one, the debunking, the pleasure of knowing something the fans in the stands didn't. The 2018 result was messier. It said the world was slightly more mysterious than the smart people had announced, that being corrected was possible even for people who had been certain for decades. He had liked the first answer because it made him feel sharp. He liked the second one for a reason he couldn't name yet, something to do with how Grandpa's whole block, this cosmopolitan stretch of duplexes and vegetable gardens and four languages on one porch, ran on nights when the rim looked bigger, on small hot streaks of luck that the record books would never confirm.

Marlowe missed his next two. Kolton pointed at the screen with the remote like a prosecutor. "See. Cold now. Where's your evidence."

"That's one miss," Hayden said. "You're doing the exact thing with his misses that you were doing with his makes."

Mr. Hussain sipped his coffee and watched the halfcourt offense set up, unbothered, a man who had watched basketball since before either paper existed. "In Karachi we had a player, name I won't say, who once made eleven in a row and then missed eleven. What do your researchers say about that?"

"I'd want to see the whole season," Elijah said. "Not just the night you remember."

Mr. Hussain considered this, nodded once, the way he nodded at weather.

The fourth quarter came down to it, as fourth quarters do. Marlowe caught the ball in the corner with nine seconds left, a shooter who had been hot and then cold and was now, for one possession, neither. Elijah leaned forward without deciding to. He did not know what he believed about the hot hand, only that he believed the question, and that seemed like the sturdier thing to carry into the fall. Grandpa's dent held him anyway. The ball went up.

story:
Elijah stood in line at the bank with his first paycheque in his jacket pocket, folded twice, which the teller would probably disapprove of. He had been employed at the garden centre for three weeks, hauling bags of soil and occasionally steering elderly customers toward the more expensive mulch, and now he wanted to deposit the cheque and open a savings account, in that order, before he lost his nerve.

Ahead of him, a man argued with a teller about a hold placed on a cheque, and behind him, someone's toddler dismantled a pen chained to the deposit-slip table. Elijah unfolded his paycheque to read it again. The gross pay said four hundred and twelve dollars. The deposit amount said considerably less. Between those two numbers sat a column of subtractions: income tax, something called CPP, something else called EI. He had understood, in a vague way, that taxes existed, the way he understood that weather existed. Seeing them itemized on his own money felt more personal.

His phone buzzed. It was Draven, texting a photo of his own pay stub from the supermarket where he'd started work in Montreal, where his family had moved in June. Elijah squinted at it in line. The deductions looked wrong. There was income tax, fine, but no CPP. Instead there was something with "QPP" in the name, and a parental insurance premium where Elijah's stub said Employment Insurance. He texted back: "yours is broken." Draven replied: "quebec's not broken, it's just quebec."

Elijah remembered the summer before grade eight, when Draven still lived four houses down and the two of them had run a snow-cone stand out of Draven's driveway, splitting a pitcher of syrup-water they'd bought with Draven's mother's money. They had charged a dollar a cone and Draven had insisted on keeping seventy cents because it was his driveway and his pitcher, and Elijah had called him an egoist, a word he'd just learned, and Draven had looked it up and accepted it as a compliment. That was the extent of their prior financial education.

At the counter, the teller stamped the deposit and slid a receipt back to him. At the bottom, in smaller print, an amount of sales tax had been added to a bookkeeping fee he hadn't known he'd be charged, provincial and federal, both listed separately, like the fee itself wasn't insult enough. He signed the receipt. The numbers on it felt like a language everyone else had been quietly speaking his whole life.

Outside, he sat on the low wall by the ATM and called Draven instead of texting. "Okay, explain yours," he said. Draven read out his stub: income tax, then the Quebec pension plan, then the parental insurance plan. "So outside Quebec you get CPP and EI on your stub," Draven said, "and here it's their own pension plan and their own parental insurance instead. It's not more money, it's just a different list."

"I was going to say you were being parochial about it," Elijah said. "Only caring about your own province's stub."

"I am being parochial about it. It's my stub."

Elijah laughed, and something settled in him that was not quite a conclusion. He had walked into the bank thinking taxes were a single deduction, one clean subtraction, and walked out having counted at least three, plus a sales tax on the way out the door, plus whatever Quebec was doing to Draven, and he still couldn't have said where any of it went or whether it was fair. His father, when Elijah had grumbled about the missing dollars at dinner, had said the deductions allay a future worry, which Elijah found too abstract to be satisfying, and possibly the kind of thing adults said instead of admitting they also found the forms confusing. He owed eleven dollars less than he thought he had saved toward the laptop he wanted. That, at least, was concrete.

He texted Anisa, who had done a co-op placement at an accounting office and filed a tax return that spring, and asked whether the return gave the money back. She wrote back a long message with the phrase "sometimes some of it" in the middle, which was either reassuring or the opposite. He put the phone in his pocket and looked at the deposit slip in his hand, the account number freshly stamped across it, his own number, in a bank, in a country that had apparently been taking its share since his very first thirty hours of shoveling mulch.

A pigeon landed on the wall beside him and considered the receipt. Elijah folded it into quarters and stood up. "Not yours," he told it.

story:
The kiln in Grandpa's garage still smelled of the last firing, a dry mineral heat that clung to the shelves even after two days with the lid open. Jaxon set his two clay bodies on the workbench side by side: the bag of rough terracotta Grandpa had left him, and the small sealed block of white porcelain clay he had bought with his own money at the art supply store in town. He was going to make a mug. Grandma's favourite one had shattered on the kitchen tiles in March, a blue and white thing she had carried from room to room for thirty years, and her birthday was in eleven days.

"You can't just pick the pretty one?" Emerson had biked over after texting asking if there was actually a kiln in a garage, which he refused to believe until he saw it, squat and beige in the corner like a washer with opinions.

"The pretty one is porcelain," Jaxon said. "It's what her old mug was, basically. But it's harder to work with. And I've only ever used the terracotta."

Emerson picked up the porcelain block and turned it over, reading the label. His lips moved a little, the way they did when he was decoding something. "It says here earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius," he said. "And porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees." He looked up. "So which one is earthenware?"

"The terracotta, I think. That's basically what it is." Jaxon took the block back. So they could not go in together. That much he could hold onto, even if the rest felt like standing at the edge of a pool. He had watched Grandpa fire the kiln twice, and Grandpa had let him stack the shelves once, but Grandpa was in the hospital until Thursday, and Thursday was cutting it close, and the firing schedule was suddenly entirely his.

They wedged the clay on the canvas-covered table, pushing air pockets out with the heels of their hands. The terracotta gave in easily, familiar as bread dough. The porcelain was softer, almost sticky, and it kept taking the print of his fingerprints so that the surface undulated faintly wherever he had gripped it, tiny ridges like wind over water. He tried to pull a cylinder on Grandpa's old wheel, the one with the foot pedal, and the porcelain slumped twice before he got a wall that stood.

"It hates you," Emerson said, watching from a plastic stool with a bag of sunflower seeds.

"It doesn't hate me. It just doesn't forgive you." That was the difference, he was starting to think, though he couldn't have said it out loud without sounding like a fortune cookie. The terracotta forgave. You could slap it back into a ball and start over and it barely remembered. The porcelain remembered everything. He liked that about it and it terrified him in equal measure.

He centered a new ball and opened it with his thumbs. His mind kept splitting into two people, the way it did when he was arguing with himself and losing track of which side he was on. One of them said: make the mug in terracotta. You know terracotta. It will be fired and glazed and wrapped by her birthday and she will use it and that is what matters, the using, the fact of it in her hand. The other one said: she carried that white mug for thirty years. If you hand her something the colour of a flowerpot, you are giving her a stand-in, and she will say it's beautiful because she is contractually obligated, the way a fiduciary is obligated to act in your interest whether or not she believes in the investment.

"Where'd you go just now?" Emerson asked.

"Nowhere. My grandpa's lawyer voice." He pulled the wall up. It held. It actually held, thin and pale as a mussel shell, taller than he meant it to be. He stopped the wheel and looked at it. Eleven days. Porcelain needed its own firing, hotter, then glaze, then another firing. Terracotta needed less but he would still be doing it alone, learning the kiln's controls by trial and prayer.

He walked to the kiln and opened the controller box. The dial and the little digital display were less mysterious than he had feared, though he took three photos of the settings and texted them to his grandfather, who replied from the hospital with a single thumbs up, which was either permission or the morphine. When Jaxon came back, Emerson was holding the finished porcelain cylinder up to the window light, turning it slowly.

"It's like the beach," Emerson said. "That white bit where the foam comes in. The littoral part, whatever it's called. We just did that word in geography."

Jaxon looked at the pale curve of the wall and saw it, the thin moving line where water met sand. He also saw every place his thumbs had wobbled. "There's a whole side that's thinner than the other," he said. "It might crack in the firing."

"Or it might not."

"Yeah." He turned the cylinder in his own hands. He had the terracotta mug he could guarantee, and this pale uncertain thing he could not, and there was no version of the next eleven days where he got both without cutting something. He set the porcelain mug carefully on the shelf above the radiator, where Grandpa kept works in progress, and reached for the terracotta.

"Both, then?" Emerson asked.

"Both. If the white one cracks, it cracks. If it doesn't, she gets to choose." He cut a lump off the terracotta bag with the wire tool and slapped it down on the canvas. "And you're staying to help stack the kiln."

Emerson cracked a sunflower seed between his teeth and dragged his stool closer to the wheel.

story:
The tour guide kept saying "home" as in, welcome home, this could be your home, and Avery kept hearing it as a question. She stood near the back of the cluster outside the admissions building, holding the folder they had given her at check-in, smelling cut grass and the faint diesel of a maintenance cart rolling past. November light came through the elms the way it did in the brochures, which she suspected was not a coincidence.

"So are you doing it?" Courtney asked her, in the tone of someone who had already decided. Courtney wanted Early Decision, wanted it the way other people wanted a prom date, and she had spent the train ride down reciting the statistics from a forum she trusted more than the school's own website. "November fifteenth. One school, one answer, done by December. Think of the senior year we'd have."

"Binding," Mikhail said. He was standing on the low stone wall, balancing with his arms out, because that was Mikhail. "I looked it up last night. It's binding. If they let you in and the aid is okay, you have to go, and you have to pull every other application."

"That's the point," Courtney said.

"That's the risk," Mikhail said, and hopped down.

Avery had known the rule, technically. But hearing it out loud on this lawn, under these particular elms, made it a different object, the way a city on a map becomes a city you are standing in. She turned the folder over in her hands. Her mother had said, at the kitchen table in October, "We'll figure out the money when we see the money," and had not seemed to hear her own sentence.

They followed the guide into a dorm, up three flights of stairs that smelled like microwave popcorn and someone's vanilla candle. In the hallway a boy in a bathrobe was arguing with a printer, slapping its side, saying "not now, Brendan," to it as though it were a person. Courtney asked the guide about the psychology program. Mikhail asked about the ratio of washing machines to students, which he claimed was the only statistic that predicted quality of life. Avery asked nothing. She was listening to herself not asking, which was a habit she was starting to notice, a kind of nascent suspicion that the questions she avoided were the real ones.

Outside again, they crossed a quad where two students were throwing a Frisbee badly on purpose, egging each other into worse and worse catches. Mr. Asante, who had driven the minivan and who coached debate and asked questions instead of giving answers, fell into step beside her. "What did you learn in there?" he said.

"That the laundry situation is dire."

"Mm," he said, and waited, because that was his whole method.

"That if I apply Early Decision here, and they take me, and the aid is acceptable, I have to come," she said. "I withdraw everything else. I only ever see one offer."

"And what do you make of that?"

"I don't know yet." She was surprised by how easily she said it, and how true it felt. Courtney's version of applying was confident, a single door kicked open. Mikhail's was defensive, keep every door ajar. Avery had been trying to pick a side, and standing here, she found she didn't want either one alone. She wanted to love a school and still see the numbers, to commit and to compare, and the rule said those were different rooms.

Mr. Asante nodded as though she had said all of that out loud. "There's a financial aid office in that building," he said. "It's open. Courtney's already inside, actually, asking about merit scholarships." And she was, visible through the glass, leaning over the desk with her whole body, the way she leaned into everything.

Avery went in. The woman at the counter gave her a sheet with sample packages, and Avery read them standing up, slowly, the way she read poems. Grant, loan, work-study, the small print where the real sentence lived. She couldn't make the numbers mean anything certain, because they were samples, because every family was different, because the whole system was an epistemology problem: how could you know a thing that only existed after you committed to it? She caught herself enjoying the question, which was probably a bad sign, or maybe the best one.

When she came out, Mikhail and Courtney were on the steps arguing about whether certainty was worth anything if you paid for it with options. They both turned to her.

"Regular," Courtney said, "you have to do Early. Tell her."

"You should wait," Mikhail said. "Tell her."

"Can you guys just hold on?" Avery said. She sat down on the step between them, put the folder on her knees, and took out the pen from her check-in packet. On the back of the financial aid sheet, in the margin, she wrote the deadline for Early Decision and, an inch below it, the deadline for Regular, and looked at the two dates side by side. "I'm going to call my mom from the van," she said, and tapped the paper twice with the pen.

story:
Emilie counted the eggs in the cooler twice, because the first count had to be wrong. It wasn't. There were none. The pancake recipe lay open on the picnic table, weighted with a flat stone against the wind, and its second instruction sat there like an accusation: two eggs, beaten. Around her the campsite held its ordinary morning, her mother still asleep in the tent, her father squatting at the fire ring arranging kindling with the patience of a man who believed breakfast would simply appear.

She had volunteered for this. Last night, around the fire, she had said she'd cook, and her mother had looked at her for a long moment before saying fine, and Emilie had understood that fine to mean something closer to a test she hadn't agreed to fail. The whole spring had been like that, her mother's expectations dissolving into hints, and Emilie's responses dissolving into defensive silences, until the fight in May about the dropped course, the one where her mother said she never finishes what she starts and Emilie walked out to Florent's house and didn't come back until dark. That was the fight nobody had mentioned since. The pancakes were supposed to be the unmentioning, the quiet repair.

She had flour, milk, the last of the sugar, a dented tin of baking powder, and butter softening in its paper on the table's sunlit end. She had set all of it out before beginning, arranged in a neat row, because some video she'd watched weeks ago had insisted on it and the orderliness had appealed to her, the way a clean page does before writing. She'd even felt a small pride in the arrangement. Now she looked down the row and saw the gap where the eggs should have been, obvious as a missing tooth, and understood that she had admired the display without actually checking it. The row was a picture of readiness, not readiness itself.

The camp store was a twenty minute walk back down the road, and the walk gave her time. A car passed her, then another, and she thought about Florent, who cooked at his grandmother's on Sundays and moved through the kitchen like he knew where everything was at all times. Once, watching him, she had asked why he laid out little bowls of everything before he started, and he had shrugged and said, "Mise en place. It's French, it means putting in place. You measure and prep everything before you cook." She had thought it sounded fussy then, a performance of diligence. Now the word came back to her with a different weight, and she turned it over as the gravel crunched under her sandals, feeling the difference between knowing a phrase and knowing what it was for. Florent didn't arrange his bowls so the kitchen would look serious. He did it so that halfway through, with his hands full of batter, he would never discover a missing thing.

At the store she bought eggs and, because she was there, a bag of apples, and on the walk back she let herself remember the May fight from her mother's side, which she had refused to do at the time. Her mother hadn't said you never finish anything as an insult, maybe, but as a fear, the way you name a foreboding out loud hoping to make it smaller. And Emilie's walking out that night had been its own kind of unfinished thing, a sentence abandoned in the middle. She didn't want to absolve herself with pancakes. She wanted, she decided somewhere between the second bend in the road and the third, to be the kind of person who checked the eggs, which was a smaller thing than the kind of person who finishes everything, and possibly a more honest one. Though she wasn't sure those were really different kinds of person, or whether her mother would see the difference, or whether she was even being fair to herself, and she let all of that sit unresolved because the road was arriving at the campsite whether she finished thinking or not.

Her father had the fire going, small and steady under the grate. Her mother was out of the tent now, hair tied up, watching Emilie come up the path with the little paper sack. Emilie put the eggs in their place at the end of her row, cracked two of them into a bowl, and beat them until they were uniform and pale. She did not announce what she'd learned. She mixed the batter, watched for the bubbles that meant the first side was done, and flipped the pancake in one motion that surprised her by working.

Her mother took the first plate and ate standing up, looking at the lake. "These are good," she said, and after a while, "you went back for eggs." It wasn't a question, and Emilie answered it anyway, saying yes, she'd forgotten them, she'd walked to the store. Her mother nodded and ate another pancake and said nothing more, and the silence between them felt different from the other silences, though Emilie couldn't have said exactly how. The morning went on, the fire ticking, the lake flat and bright.

Later Emilie washed the bowl in the campsite's cold tap, alone, her sleeves pushed up, the water numbing her fingers. She looked at the wet table where her row of ingredients had been, everything used, everything accounted for, and started drying the spoons one by one.

story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and cut lilies, and behind the folding doors the band was already playing the march that everyone in North America walks to. Kael stood beside Natalie in the line of graduates, humming the tune under his mortarboard, and she found herself humming it too before she noticed what she was doing.

"Do you ever wonder where that came from?" he asked. "Like, who decided this is the walking song. Did somebody vote on it?"

Natalie said she didn't know, and then she couldn't stop wondering, because the tune felt older than her school, older than the school board, older than the town itself, and nobody had ever told her where it started. She was two years younger than everyone around her, having skipped a grade so long ago that it barely came up anymore, except at moments like this when she felt the chronology of her life slide slightly out of step with everyone else's. Danica, ahead of her in line, turned around and tugged Natalie's tassel straight without being asked. "You're crooked," Danica said. "We can't have that."

They walked. The bleachers were full and the air conditioning was losing its argument with four hundred bodies. Somewhere in the rows, Natalie's mother lifted a phone. When the principal said her name, she crossed the stage, shook hands, and heard, faintly, her mother's whoop, which she would deny later and which she was glad of anyway.

The party afterward was at Danica's house, in the backyard, where strings of lights had been hung between the fence and the maple. Natalie arrived with her gown stuffed in a tote bag and her phone at eight percent. She found Kael by the cooler, filling a cup for a boy whose hands were full of cake, and she asked him whether he'd ever looked up the march.

"I looked it up during the ceremony," Kael admitted. "I was bored. It's Elgar. Pomp and Circumstance March Number One." He said it had premiered in Liverpool, in 1901, which meant people had been walking slowly to it for more than a century before any of them were born.

"Liverpool," Natalie repeated. "It's not even from here."

"It's from a country most of us have never been to, and we made it our ritual anyway." Kael shrugged. "Somebody in some auditorium in, I don't know, Ohio, played it once, and it just catalyzed everything. Now it's the tradition. Nobody remembers deciding."

Natalie sat with that while the party went on around her, but not for long, because sitting with things was not really how parties worked. Danica pulled her toward the lawn where people were dancing badly, and she danced badly too, and then she sat on the porch steps with Mr. Tehrani, the physics teacher from across the street who had been invited because Danica's family invited everyone, and he was eating cake alone and pretending he liked it that way. She got him a fork, because he was managing with a napkin, and he thanked her with a kind of surprised warmth.

"Are you sorry to be finished?" he asked her. "You started early. You finish early."

"I'm not sure what I am," Natalie said. "Everyone keeps saying it's the end of something, but it doesn't feel like an ending. It feels like the middle that everyone agreed to call an ending." She told him about the march, how it was written in England and premiered in Liverpool in 1901, and how everyone here walked to it anyway, generation after generation, without knowing. "Maybe that's what a tradition is. Something borrowed so long ago it stops being borrowed."

"Or it's still borrowed," Mr. Tehrani said, "and we just stopped keeping the receipt." He held up his fork in something like a toast.

Later, when the sky over the houses had gone the deep blue that only happens in June, Natalie found Danica at the fence, alone for a moment, looking tired in the specific way of someone who had organized too much and thanked too many people. Natalie brought her a cup of water, not punch, and stood beside her without saying anything at first.

"You're going to that school in the fall," Danica said. "The one eight hours away."

"Six and a half."

"Six and a half." Danica drank the water. "Promise you'll come back for something. Anything. Christmas. My birthday. I don't care what."

Natalie thought about the march, how it had traveled from Liverpool across an ocean and a century and ended up in a gymnasium in a town it was never meant for, and how that had turned out to be the whole point of it. She put her arm through Danica's. "I'll come back," she said. "I don't know for what yet. But I'll come back."

The lights on the fence swung a little in the wind, and from the yard behind them someone had put the march on the speaker as a joke, and people were singing along to the trio section, badly, with their arms around each other, and Natalie stayed where she was and listened to the whole thing through.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
The flood in the school auditorium had been sudden, a pipe gone in the ceiling over the stage, and the one-act festival was in nine days, so when Elizabeth's grandmother said that Mr. Holloway had offered his converted carriage house, Elizabeth said yes before she had seen it. She saw it on a Tuesday after school: a long, bright room with a polished floor in the middle and no stage at all, no curtain, no place where the audience could be assumed to sit. Mr. Holloway had already set out folding chairs, and he had set them out on all four sides, a full ring around the empty center, because that was the only way to fit the forty seats the festival required. Elizabeth stood in the middle of the floor with her binder against her chest and understood that every movement she had planned was wrong.

She had blocked the whole play in the school gym, imagining a stage with the audience in front of it. Graysen entered left and crossed downstage right; Rylee stood center and delivered the long confession while Graysen circled her; the final tableau faced front, both of them turned toward an audience that no longer existed in one direction. She walked the old blocking alone in the carriage house, counting. When she stood where Rylee stood and faced where Rylee faced, an entire quarter of the chairs looked at her back. She turned to give those chairs her face and lost the other three walls.

"That's why they keep moving," she said out loud, to nobody, and then she laughed at herself, embarrassed, but the thought held. On a stage in the round, the audience sat on all sides, and the director had to keep the actors moving so that no section of chairs only ever saw their backs. It was not a style choice. It was arithmetic, or geometry, or something more like fairness: every person who had paid and driven out here deserved a front, at least sometimes, and it was her job to hand the fronts around.

Rehearsal the next evening was worse than she had feared. Rylee had learned her confessional monologue facing one way, and facing one way had become somatic for her, tied into her breathing, so that when Elizabeth rotated her a quarter turn every eight lines, the speech went flat and Rylee's hands stopped knowing what to do. "It's in my body," Rylee said, not complaining, reporting. "If I turn, I forget the words." Graysen, who had circled smoothly, was little help, because he circled too smoothly, like a ceiling fan, and Elizabeth realized that motion for its own sake could desensitize an audience just as thoroughly as stillness. Movement had to mean something, or the chairs might as well be watching weather.

She tried three new plans that night and abandoned all three. The fourth she drafted at her grandmother's kitchen table, on graph paper, with the room drawn as a square and arrows for the actors, and her grandmother put tea beside her without asking questions, which Elizabeth understood as a form of love. The plan was no longer a picture to be seen from one side. It was a rotation, a slow distribution of faces, and she had to admit, in the margin, in pencil, that she did not yet know whether the audience would feel cared for or merely managed, whether being given a front was the same as being given attention. She wrote "uncertain" and left it.

Friday, the real problem arrived, and it was not geometry. Graysen and Rylee disagreed about the final scene, the one where his character decides to leave. Graysen wanted a long exit, walking the full perimeter, so that every section of the ring saw his face during the goodbye. Rylee wanted him gone fast, a straight cut across the center, because the abandonment, she said, should land like a slap and not like a tour. They argued for ten minutes, respectfully at first, then less so, and Elizabeth felt the temptation to impose one of the plans by authority, since the director was, she supposed, some kind of judge. Instead she made them run it both ways and stood in different chairs herself, one section at a time, watching.

From the north chairs, the perimeter exit was devastating: he circled away, and Rylee's face held the whole time. From the east chairs, the straight cut was better, faster, crueler. She understood then that she was not looking for the right answer but conducting an arbitration between two audiences, or between two truths about the same moment, and she would have to choose without being able to stand in every chair at once. She chose the long exit, but she cut it short on the last third, turned him once more toward Rylee's face, and let the very last steps happen with his back to the south section only, because somebody, somewhere, had to watch him go, and she decided it could be the south.

At the Saturday run-through, with Mr. Holloway and her grandmother and four neighbor ladies in the ring, Elizabeth sat in a different seat for each act, keeping score on her knee with small tallies, front, front, profile, back. Afterward Rylee found her stacking chairs and said, "The turning doesn't break the speech anymore. I got used to it." Graysen carried the last two chairs to the wall and asked, quiet, so only Elizabeth heard, "Did anybody only see my back?" Elizabeth looked at her tally sheet, at the small uneven columns, and handed it to him without a word. He read it, and folded it once, and put it in his pocket.

story:
The intake desk at the Riverside Clinic had two stacks of paper, one green and one white, and Megan had learned in her first week that the green ones were waivers and the white ones were everything else. She stamped forms, checked insurance cards, and sent patients to the waiting room with a laminated number. The job paid twelve dollars an hour. She wanted the front desk coordinator position that would open in September, which paid fifteen and came with a set of keys, and to get it she had to get through the summer without a complaint from a patient or a nurse.

At three on a Thursday a woman arrived with her son, who was seventeen and needed his wisdom teeth out. Megan slid the consent packet across the counter and offered a pen. The boy, whose name tag from his own job at the hardware store said HENRI, read the form standing up while his mother went to park the car. He read it for a long time. Then he said, "This part about nerve injury. It says permanent numbness may occur. How often?"

Megan had never been asked that. The form listed the risks of the procedure and the alternatives, including doing nothing, and it listed the benefits too, but it did not list numbers. "I don't know," she said. "I can ask the nurse to come out."

"That's it?" Henri said. "I'm supposed to sign this, and the answer is a nurse might know?"

The nurse on duty was a woman named Ms. Rivera, who had worked at the clinic longer than the vending machine. Megan found her in the back and explained the situation, and Ms. Rivera came to the desk, took the form from Henri's hand, and said, "Ask me anything on there. That's what it's for. Informed consent means you agree to the treatment only after you've been told the risks, the benefits, and the alternatives, in words you can understand. If any of it isn't clear, that's on us, not you."

"Informed consent," Henri repeated. "Okay. The numbness."

Ms. Rivera explained the numbness in plain sentences, then went through what the surgery would do for him and what would happen if he left the teeth alone. Henri asked two more questions, one about anesthesia and one about cost. Then he signed, dated it, and gave Megan back the pen. "You should get a tip jar," he said. "For people who read."

Later that week a problem surfaced. A patient named Ally, who had come in for a shoulder injection in June, called to say she had signed a form she never read and now wanted to dispute the charge for a second procedure she said nobody described to her. There was a copy of the form in the file. Megan pulled it and found the signature, but the file also contained a note in Ms. Rivera's handwriting that the patient had seemed rushed and that the alternatives had been summarized rather than discussed. The clinic's office manager wanted the charge to stand, on the grounds that a signature was a signature. Megan, who had been told to draft the reply letter as a test for the coordinator job, sat with the file for most of her lunch break.

She wrote the letter that afternoon and kept a copy. Dear Ally, it began. Thank you for your call on Tuesday. I have reviewed the forms from your visit on June 14. You are right that your signature appears on the consent for the second procedure. However, our own record notes that the discussion of alternatives was brief, and our standard is that consent is informed only when the risks, benefits, and alternatives have been explained in language the patient can understand. On that basis, we are cancelling the charge for the second procedure, and we would like to schedule a conversation with Ms. Rivera before any future treatment so that everything is covered properly. She signed it with her name and the words Intake Desk, and the office manager read it, frowned at it, and then said, "Fine. Send it. It's cheaper than a complaint to the state board."

Megan understood the two positions without much difficulty. The manager thought in terms of terms and conditions, liability, what the paper proved. Ms. Rivera thought in terms of what the patient actually knew. Megan had assumed for most of the summer that these were the same thing, that a signature closed the matter, and the letter was her way of saying they were not. What she could not settle was where the line fell. A clinic could not run if every conversation had to be transcribed, and a patient could not be protected by a form alone. The chronology of Ally's file, signature first, doubt second, was the whole story in miniature, and Megan could not rewrite it, only respond to it. Her somatic complaint about the situation, a tightness behind the ribs that no form had a box for, eased when the manager said to send the letter.

Henri came back the following Tuesday for his post-op check, cheeks still faintly swollen, carrying a paper bag of soft candy he had bought, he said, to propitiate the dental gods. He put three pieces on the counter for Megan. "Numbness," he reported, "temporary. I asked. Everything temporary. Also my mom says you're the only person in this town who reads."

"I read for a living now," Megan said. "Twelve dollars an hour."

"Fifteen in September?"

"That's the rumor." She stamped his form, gave him a laminated number, and pointed at the waiting room, where the vending machine was refusing quarters again and a toddler was conducting an investigation into its coin slot. Henri picked up his number, sat down beside the toddler, and began explaining, in plain words the child could almost understand, the risks and benefits of further digging.

story:
The game had been going for an hour before anyone thought to question the television, and by then it was too late to question it politely. Elijah sat on the floor of his grandfather's living room with his back against the armchair, between Antony and Imran, all three of them holding paper plates of rice and chicken that had gone cold because nobody wanted to look down. His grandfather occupied the good chair. Mr. Sow, who had come over from next door carrying a bowl of groundnuts and an opinion about everything, occupied the sofa with the authority of a man who considered himself a second referee.

The disputed play happened in the second quarter. A receiver caught the ball at the sideline, twisted, dragged one toe along the chalk, and fell out of bounds with his hands still raised. The official on the far side threw his hat. Half the room roared. Mr. Sow stood up, pointed at the screen with a groundnut, and announced that the receiver had been out of bounds before the ball arrived, that the official was blind, and that if the station had any decency it would show the play again.

"Show it again," Antony said, leaning toward the set as though proximity could produce the image. "They do that. They replay things."

"Not this station," the grandfather said. "This is an old broadcast, my friend. They show it once and it is gone."

Imran, who had been quiet most of the afternoon, watching the room the way he watched everything, said, "Then we decide ourselves." He got up and stood close to the screen with his phone held out, ready to record whatever came next, because the halftime show was starting in four minutes and after that the second half would bury the argument under new ones. That was the deadline nobody said out loud: settle it before kickoff, or argue about it for the rest of the day.

Elijah had learned the fact a month earlier, in a library book about television he had picked up off a cart because the cover was falling off and he felt sorry for it. He hadn't expected to keep it, but it had stayed with him the way certain things do, lodging somewhere between memory and decoration. Now he looked around the room, at Mr. Sow's hat still pointing at the screen, at his grandfather's patient hands folded over his stomach, at Imran's phone blinking, and he understood that what he had was not trivia. It was a way of framing the argument, and framing the argument might end it.

"They can show it again," Elijah said. "It's been possible for a long time. The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game, on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by a director named Tony Verna." He said it evenly, without the triumph he half wanted, because he had learned from his father that being right loudly cost more than it paid.

Mr. Sow lowered the groundnut. "This game?"

"No, no. A different game. Long ago. But the same idea. Since then, a play doesn't have to be gone when it's gone."

From the armchair, the grandfather made a sound that was not quite a laugh. He had been a schoolteacher for thirty-one years and had retired with the suspicion that machines were abrogating the authority that people had once earned the hard way, by watching closely and committing to what they saw. In his day, he said now, the game ended when the game ended, and arguments about it were carried on for weeks in the market, in the letters page, over Sunday rice, and this was not a flaw in the arrangement. It was the arrangement. He looked at Elijah, and there was something in the look that Elijah could not read as approval or disapproval, only attention.

"So the machine remembers for us," the grandfather said. "And what do we become?"

Imran, who had watched Elijah say the fact and watched Mr. Sow absorb it, felt the argument loosen in the room the way a knot loosens when you stop pulling. He thought of his own father, who kept a torn ticket stub from a match neither of them had attended, his father's father having described it so many times that Imran could almost see it, could almost dispute it. Maybe that was what the replay had replaced: the telling, the disagreeing, the slow friable handing down of what happened, wearing away a little with each telling and gaining something else. He did not say this. He said, "Three minutes," and held up the phone.

Mr. Sow sat back down. He was not a man who conceded, but he was a man who could be redirected. "December 7, 1963," he said slowly, turning the date over. "That's a long time to be able to see a thing twice and still not agree on it."

"That's true," Elijah said, and found he meant it in a way he hadn't expected. He had brought the fact out like a tool, and it had opened something, but it had not settled anything, because the play they were arguing about was already gone and no system devised by any director was reaching back to get it. The truth of the fact and the usefulness of the fact were turning out to be two different things, and he held both of them without being able to make them meet.

The halftime show ended. The teams lined up. Mr. Sow reached for another groundnut, looked once more at the place on the screen where the receiver's toe had touched the chalk, and said, "Out of bounds. I don't care what any machine would have said." Imran raised his phone and hit record anyway.

story:
The coffee shop had replaced its register with a kiosk the size of a small television, and Mathis watched it tell Kohen that his medium latte would be nine dollars and forty cents. Kohen tapped his card without looking. It was only when Izaiah, ordering the same thing, got charged five seventy-five that anyone thought to check the screen.

"It says the price," the cashier said, when Mathis pointed at the difference. She was new, or the kiosk was new to her, and she kept glancing at it the way people glance at a supervisor. "It wouldn't print it if it wasn't the charge."

"The menu says five seventy-five," Mathis said. "Right there. On the wall."

She looked at the wall, then back at the kiosk, and the kiosk won. "The system calculates it," she said. "I'd have to go by the system." She offered Kohen a napkin as a form of apology, or perhaps as a way of ending the conversation.

They took the corner table by the window, where Mr. Rodríguez was already sitting with a book he wasn't reading. He had been their history teacher until June, and he still occupied the corner table most afternoons like a retired diplomat. He had watched the whole exchange with the turbid patience of a man who had decided not to intervene.

"That machine has overcharged me twice this month," he said. "Both times I paid. Then I stood outside feeling like a character in a parable."

"My mom did something like that on Saturday," Kohen said. "The GPS told her to turn onto Alder Street, and there was a barricade, and an actual sign that said ROAD CLOSED, and she turned anyway. Then she sat there honking at the barricade like it would move."

"She believed the app over her own eyes," Izaiah said.

"There's a name for it," Mathis said. He had spent a chunk of the summer reading about systems, partly for a college essay he was avoiding writing and partly because his father had been laid off in the spring and the word "automation" had begun to appear at dinner in the tones people reserve for weather. "Automation bias. It's the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct."

Mr. Rodríguez lowered his book an inch.

"Which is what she did," Mathis went on. "The sign was contradicting information, and it was correct, and she ignored it anyway. Same as your cashier. The wall menu is correct, and she ignored it, because the kiosk suggested something else." He found that the two events, which he had been holding separately all afternoon, folded into each other neatly, the way his philosophy teacher liked to say small cases could subsume larger ones, the personal swallowed by the pattern.

"So it's not chicanery," Izaiah said, testing the word out. "Nobody's conning us. The machine isn't evil."

"That's the strange part," Mathis said. "If someone were cheating us on purpose, we'd be angry, and anger is easy. This is worse. We're doing it to ourselves. We like being told what to do by things that sound certain."

Kohen had gone back to the counter. Through the glass they watched him argue, point at the menu, point at his receipt, point at the receipt again. The cashier looked at the kiosk between every sentence, as though checking whether it still permitted his refund.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Mathis said. "Your mom's GPS is right almost all the time. The kiosk is right almost all the time. So the habit of trusting them isn't stupid. It's mostly rational. The problem is that we can't tell the almost from the always, because nothing about the machine changes when it's wrong. It's just as confident at nine forty as at five seventy-five."

"So you don't trust it at all?" Mr. Rodríguez asked.

"No. That's not what I'm saying either. I'm saying I don't know where the line is, and I don't think anybody does. Maybe the answer is just checking, every time, which is exhausting, and nobody will do it."

Mr. Rodríguez turned this over with the visible effort of a man who had been hoping for a lighter afternoon. "For what it's worth," he said, "I checked the second time it overcharged me. The first time, I paid and left a tip."

Kohen returned, triumphant, holding three dollars and seventy cents in coins that the kiosk had dispensed with the solemnity of a state apology. He set them on the table and counted them twice, and while he counted, the screen at the counter lit up with a new order, and the cashier, without looking at the wall, entered it exactly as the machine had suggested.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
The flyer had said the food bank operated out of the basement of Hillcrest Seniors' Residence, but Levi hadn't pictured it properly until he was standing in it: folding tables in the common room, a hand-lettered sign taped over the piano, boxes of tinned pears stacked against a wall of floral wallpaper. Ms. Demetriou, who ran it, handed him a clipboard before he'd finished saying his name.

"You're the student volunteer. Good. Rose-Marie will show you the intake desk."

Rose-Marie turned out to be a girl from his civics class, and behind her, sorting bread with the resigned efficiency of someone who had done it many times, was Ema. Levi's stomach dropped. He and Ema had not spoken since the argument in the library, the one about the group project he had abandoned to study for exams, and neither of them had moved to fix it.

"Clipboard," Rose-Marie said, pointing. "You check people in. Name, household size, note anything they can't eat. Don't lose the pen."

The morning was quiet until it wasn't. An old man wanted to know why the pasta sauce had changed brands. A woman with a walker asked, twice, whether the fish was fresh. Then the debit machine went down, and a line formed, and Ms. Demetriou disappeared into the back to phone the office, leaving the three of them.

"I'll write the totals by hand," Ema said, already pulling a sheet toward her.

"I have the clipboard," Levi said. "That's intake. Totals are mine."

Ema's pen stopped. "You weren't here last month. There's an order to it."

"There's a line forming. We don't have time for your order."

Rose-Marie looked between them, then took the debit machine and started coaxing it back to life, which left Levi and Ema standing over one sheet of paper with two pens. It was Rose-Marie who negotiated the detente, without ever naming it that way: "She writes, he adds, I run cards. Move."

They moved. Levi called names off the clipboard and read quantities aloud, and Ema's handwriting flew, and when their hands collided reaching for the same page, she pulled back half an inch and kept writing. It worked the way a borrowed machine works, tolerably, until the machine came back.

At noon the line thinned. Levi retreated to the wall to recalibrate his whole understanding of the morning, which was not, he admitted, germane to anything, but he did it anyway. Behind him was a framed poster, curling at one corner, that he hadn't noticed in the rush. The World's First Food Bank, it read across the top, and beneath the heading, a black-and-white photograph of a man standing among stacked crates.

"You're blocking the poster," Ema said. She had come over with the totals sheet.

"Sorry." He stepped sideways instead of away. "It says St. Mary's Food Bank. Phoenix, Arizona."

"1967," Ema read, following his finger. "Founded by John van Hengel." She squinted at the small print. "It's still running. That's the whole point of it, I think. Somebody started something and it just kept going."

Levi looked at the man in the photograph, standing in a warehouse that looked much emptier than this common room, and thought about how far an idea had travelled to end up in a basement under a piano no one was allowed to play. Fifty-odd years, and here was tinned pears and a broken debit machine and two people not speaking.

"I owe you an apology," he said. "For the project. I left you and Rose-Marie with the presentation."

"I know."

"I'm not saying it was right. I'm saying I knew it was wrong while I did it, which is worse."

Ema folded the totals sheet in half, then in half again, which struck him as a way of deciding something. "You add fast," she said. "In there. Under pressure."

"My grandmother makes me do her crossword arithmetic. She lives upstairs, actually. Third floor. That's why I picked this place."

"She's the one who asked for no fish, then. The one with the walker."

"That's her. She can't know I volunteer here, by the way. She'd be mortified. She thinks needing the food bank and living here are different kinds of people, and she's one kind."

Ema looked at the door where his grandmother had gone out twenty minutes earlier, her walker clicking across the linoleum, the tinned pears heavy in her bag. "They're not different kinds," she said. "That's the thing I keep learning here."

Ms. Demetriou came back at last, phone in hand, saying the office could collect the paper totals at three, and could someone restack the pears because a resident on the main floor had leaned on the display. Levi was closest. He crouched and began rebuilding the pyramid, can by can, and Ema knelt down across from him and squared the base so the rows wouldn't slide.

"Same time next week?" Rose-Marie called from the desk.

Levi set the last can on top and looked across the pyramid at Ema, who still had the folded totals sheet in her hand and was watching him with an expression he couldn't fully read, which he decided was fair.

"Same time next week," he said.

activity: going on a first date
story:
Michael had planned the date down to the minute, which he already suspected was a mistake. He had the movie tickets in his jacket pocket, printed at home like a ransom note, and a route through the mall that passed the arcade because Alyson had once mentioned, in the middle of a chemistry lab, that she liked air hockey. He had no evidence that she still liked air hockey. He was, in fact, predicated on almost nothing except one sentence spoken over a Bunsen burner three weeks ago, and he had built an entire evening on top of it.

He found her by the fountain, where they had agreed to meet, and she was easy to find because she was laughing at something on her phone and did not see him for a full ten seconds, which gave him time to decide how to walk. He chose casual. Casual lasted four steps before he abandoned it.

"You're early," she said.

"You're earlier."

"My mom dropped me off and then went to buy a drawer organizer, so I had nowhere to be." She pocketed the phone. "Also, hi."

They did the arcade first, which turned out to be the correct order of operations, because Michael lost at air hockey three games straight and it broke whatever formality had been clinging to the evening. Alyson played with a kind of focused violence he had not anticipated. When she scored her eleventh goal she did a small bow, and a kid watching from the change machine applauded, and Michael laughed harder than he meant to.

The complication arrived at the pretzel stand. Michael reached for his wallet and found his jacket pocket occupied by a folded object that was not a wallet: the movie tickets, which was fine, except that the wallet itself had gone wherever wallets go, probably onto the counter at home next to his bus pass and his entire identity as a person with money. He stood there doing the math. The tickets were paid for. The pretzels were not. Alyson watched his face go through its small crisis and said, "I've got it," already handing over the cash, and he hated it, because the whole evening had been predicated, in his head, on him being the one who handled things.

"You can get the next one," she said. "That's how plutocracy works. Somebody's always buying."

"That's not what plutocracy means."

"I know what it means. I just like the word." She handed him his pretzel. "Consider it an ancillary benefit of dating someone with a functioning wallet."

He thought about his sister's advice from last week, which had been a single sentence delivered while she microwaved noodles: don't make it a bigger deal than it is. He had disagreed then, privately, because it was a big deal, at least to him, standing in the food court under the skylight with a girl who had beaten him at air hockey and bought him a pretzel and seemed, against all odds, to be having an okay time. The movie was in forty minutes. There was a bench by the escalators where you could sit and watch people go up and down, which was free, which mattered now.

They sat on the bench, and it was better than the movie probably would have been. She told him about her cousin's wedding, where the DJ had played the same song twice and an uncle had fallen into the dessert table, and he told her about the time he got locked in the school library overnight, which was an exaggeration of the forty minutes it had actually been, and she caught the exaggeration and made him confess to the real number, and somehow being caught made the story funnier rather than worse.

Then, on the walk toward the theater, she slowed down a little. "Can I tell you something without it being weird?"

"Probably," he said, and immediately regretted the hedging.

"Daphnee and I were talking about this, because of health class. Consent to anything, like, touching, holding hands, whatever. It can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given." She said it quickly, eyes on the mall floor. "And I'm not saying anything happened, because nothing happened. I just wanted to say it out loud, so it's a real thing between us and not a thing we're both guessing about."

Michael had heard the same sentence in the same health class and had filed it away as a rule for emergencies, something with sirens attached. He had not thought of it as a thing you could just say on a first date, plainly, the way you'd say the movie starts at seven. He understood, suddenly, that the rule wasn't only for the moment something went wrong. It was the reason nothing had to go wrong. It meant you didn't have to guess at each other, reading shoulders and silences like tea leaves, because either of you could just speak.

"That's good," he said. "I mean, yes. Obviously yes. And same, for me too."

"Okay." She exhaled, and some of the quickness went out of her voice. "Okay, cool. Also, honest update: I'm kind of exhausted. My mom's picking me up at nine outside the north entrance. Would it be terrible if we skipped the movie and just did this? Walked a loop, sat on the world's best bench again?"

He looked at the printed tickets in his pocket, all that planning reduced to fourteen dollars of paper, and found that he didn't mind at all, which surprised him, and then didn't surprise him. "The bench is the premium experience anyway," he said. "Everything else was ancillary."

She grinned. "You don't know what that word means either, do you."

They walked the long loop past the darkened storefronts, past the fountain being drained for the night, and when her mother's car pulled up to the curb Alyson turned and said, "Next time you bring the wallet, I'll bring the air hockey."
