activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Vanessa had written the play three times and hated it twice. The assignment from Mr. Pereira was specific: a ten-minute play drawn from a real moment in her own life, staged for the class in May. She had chosen the night her mother came home from the hospital with a scar hidden under her collar and said nothing about it, and Vanessa had written seven pages of the two of them not saying anything either, which Nancy, reading over her shoulder in the cafeteria, called "brave" in a way that suggested it might also be unwatchable.

The problem, as Vanessa saw it, was that she could not tell whether her dialogue was good or merely quiet. On the page, lines like "Your soup is getting cold" seemed to carry the weight of a whole unspoken diagnosis. But she had never heard anyone say them out loud, and she was beginning to suspect that the page was lying to her the way a mirror flatters you when you're the one holding it.

She asked Nancy and Leonie to come over on a Saturday, before her mother left for her shift, when the house still smelled of coffee and the lemon cleaner she scrubbed the counters with every morning. Vanessa printed five copies of the script in the dining room, the good printer paper slightly warm from the machine. She set out water glasses and a bowl of pretzels she immediately regretted, because pretzels seemed like something a person would put out if she thought she was running a real production.

"So we just sit and read it?" Leonie asked, turning her pages face down the way she did before a test.

"It's called a table read," Vanessa said. "A read-through of the script by the cast, sitting down, before any staging. That's how you hear the dialogue."

Nancy played the mother, Leonie played Vanessa, and Vanessa read the stage directions, which felt strange, like narrating her own memory in the second person. For the first two pages it went fine. Leonie had a nice flat delivery that suited the character, and the silence Vanessa had written between speeches actually existed, in the room, as real silence, which startled her.

Then Nancy got to the line "You've always been the sagacious one, haven't you," and stopped. She looked up. "People don't say sagacious. My aunt calls me clever and my grandmother calls me too big for my boots. Nobody has ever said sagacious to me in my life."

Vanessa felt her face go hot. She had put the word in because it was the kind of word her mother would use in an argument, the kind that stigmatized Vanessa as the child, the one who was allowed to be right but not to be listened to. Except Nancy was right: it didn't sound like talk. It sounded like writing. It sounded like a line that existed to be admired on a page, and the whole reason she had gathered them at the table was to catch exactly this.

"Keep going," she said. "Don't fix anything yet."

The rest of the read-through got worse in a useful way. Leonie stumbled over a speech about the zeitgeist of the household, whatever Vanessa had meant by that, and they both laughed, not cruelly, and Vanessa wrote "cut" in the margin before Leonie had finished laughing. But then, near the end, something happened that Vanessa had not planned. Nancy read the mother's line "Your soup is getting cold," and Leonie answered with the line Vanessa had written for herself, "I made it for you," and the two lines together, spoken, in the afternoon light coming through the blinds in stripes across the table, did land. They landed so hard that Nancy paused and said quietly, "Oh. Keep that."

After they left, taking the pretzels, leaving the water glasses sweating rings on the wood, Vanessa sat with the marked-up script and thought about the difference between the two kinds of writing she'd discovered in one afternoon. The kind that performed its intelligence, and the kind that let two ordinary sentences collide and make a third thing in the air between the actors. She believed, provisionally, that the second kind was better. She was less sure about what to do with the parts of her mother that really did talk like a dictionary, whether flattening her into plain speech was honest or just another kind of editing, the kind that made real people easier to watch. She didn't know yet. She underlined the question in green ink so she would come back to it.

Her mother came downstairs in her work uniform, keys already in hand, and paused at the dining room door. "Was that your play? I heard laughing."

"It was a table read," Vanessa said. "Nancy thought a line was fake."

"Was she right?"

"Half the time."

Her mother looked at the script lying open on the table, at the margin crowded with green ink, and did not pick it up. "Will I get to hear it?"

Vanessa turned the pages back to the beginning, squared them against the tabletop, and said, "Sit down. I'll read you both parts."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
Rebecca had counted the lunch tables from the doorway of the cafeteria before she let herself walk in. Seven tables, and each one had a logic she could already guess at: the soccer girls with their cleats piled like kindling, the debate kids arguing over half a sandwich, the gamers with their screens up, the quiet table near the window where nobody talked much and everybody seemed fine with that. It was her third day at Alden Ridge High, and so far she had eaten standing at the vending machines, which was starting to feel less like a choice and more like a confession.

The move itself had been her mother's idea, though nobody had put it that way. The job was better here, the house was cheaper, and Rebecca had watched her parents beseech her, in their restrained way, to see the upside: a fresh start, a school with a better robotics program, a town with an actual river in it. She had said yes to all of it because the alternative was saying what she actually felt, which was that she had spent four years building a life in Hartsville and now the whole structure was being lifted and set down somewhere it had no foundation.

In homeroom, a boy named Grayden had lent her a pencil without being asked, and when she tried to return it he waved it off. "Keep it. We have a surplus." He said it like a statistician reporting on national reserves, and she had laughed for the first time in three days. He turned out to sit near the window table at lunch, and on Thursday she made herself carry her tray in his direction, then lost her nerve at the last second and took the empty seat at the end instead, close enough to hear them and far enough to pretend she hadn't aimed.

They were arguing about the cafeteria itself. A girl named Emmanuel, who had a lanyard covered in enamel pins, was saying that the tables proved something. "It's not cliques," she said. "It's homophily. Sociologists, Lazarsfeld and Merton, 1954. The tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves. It's not a conspiracy, it's just how it works." Grayden pushed his milk around. "So it's fate, then. Comfortable fate." Emmanuel shrugged. "It's a finding, not a verdict."

Rebecca wrote the word on her hand during fifth period, partly to remember it and partly because her old friends would have found it funny, the way they had found everything funny, and she wanted a small proof that she was still a person who found things funny. Hartsville had worked exactly the way Lazarsfeld and Merton described, though she'd never had a term for it: six girls who all ran cross country, all hated the same teacher, all dressed from the same two stores. It had felt less like a choice than like water finding its level. That was the comfort of it, and also, she was beginning to suspect, the ceiling.

By Friday she had located her level, or something like it. The window table tolerated her presence, then absorbed it. Grayden showed her the lab where the robotics team met, and Ms. Quinn, who coached it, looked at the bridge design Rebecca pulled up on her phone and said only, "Tuesday, four o'clock," which Rebecca understood to be the highest available compliment. Emmanuel walked her to the bus loop and pointed out which houses had dogs that would charge the fence and which merely surveilled. It was fast. It was almost suspiciously fast, and Rebecca kept waiting for someone to reveal a condition.

That weekend her old friend called, and the call went the way calls go when two people are standing in different rooms of their lives. There was a party she'd missed, a story that needed six layers of context she no longer had, a silence at the end that neither of them filled. "It's like you moved planets," her friend said, not unkindly, and Rebecca said the wifi was terrible here, and they both let that stand for what it was. Afterward she sat on her new bed in her new room and thought that the old table in Hartsville had not been impermeable exactly, but it had never once needed to open, and she had liked it that way, and liking it that way was the thing she couldn't quite forgive herself for.

On Tuesday she stayed late in the lab, and Ms. Quinn came around the bench, examined Rebecca's truss joints, and said, "You're a pragmatist. You build for the load, not for the elegance." Rebecca turned the structure in her hands. She had been called worse. It occurred to her that fitting in here might be the same kind of competence: find the load, build for the load. Efficient, even wise, according to two sociologists from 1954. And yet something in her balked at taking it entirely as instruction, because the window table had not chosen her for any quality of hers. They had chosen her because she was near, and quiet, and carried a pencil Grayden had granted her. She had walked into a room, read the pattern, and followed it. Whether that was intelligence or surrender she genuinely did not know.

The next Saturday she did something small and deliberate about it. She took her lunch to the table where nobody talked much, the one everyone else seemed to regard as a waiting room, and sat down across from a girl who was sketching the river through the window in a notebook with the covers bent back. The girl looked up, looked at the sketch, and turned it so Rebecca could see the whole span of it. "The light's better in the afternoon," she said. It was not an invitation and not a dismissal. It was a fact about light.

Rebecca ate her sandwich and watched the river hold its gray shine, thinking of Emmanuel's word, of Grayden's surplus pencil still in her bag, of the call she had not returned yet and might not return for a week. She didn't know if she was doing this out of principle or loneliness or the plain pleasure of sitting near a drawing. Homophily was real, and it had already worked on her twice this month, and it would probably keep working, and maybe the best she could do was notice it, sometimes, and row against it briefly, the way you test a current by heading upstream just to feel the pull. The girl added a stroke to the far bank and said, without looking up, "You'll smudge it if you put your elbow there."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
story:
The town hall had been called to discuss the new civics requirement at Sophie's school, and the folding chairs in the gymnasium were already half full by the time she found a seat near the back. She had come with a question she hadn't managed to shake since spring break, when she'd watched the news at her grandmother's house with her grandmother's tenant, a graduate student named Faris who was visiting his cousin in town. The television had shown a prime minister leaving office, and Sophie had asked, genuinely puzzled, why nobody had voted directly for him. Faris had started to answer, then stopped himself and said she should work it out, and the moment had stuck to her like a burr.

Ms. Boateng, who taught the elective in comparative government, had organized the evening around a mock question: should the town switch its youth council to elect its leader directly, or should the council choose and be able to remove its leader by a vote of the members. Sophie had signed up to speak on the direct-election side because it seemed obvious to her. The president was elected; that was what a real democracy did. She had three index cards with arguments about mandates and legitimacy, and she'd practiced them against her bedroom mirror.

Braelyn sat two rows ahead, twisting a pen between her fingers. When Ms. Boateng opened the floor, an older man near the stage stood up first and complained, in a slow grumble, that everything was rigged now, that the disaffected kids on the youth council would just keep voting each other out and nothing would ever get done. A woman near him called him an apologist for whatever it was he was defending, and it took Sophie a moment to realize the woman meant he was defending the old system, the one where the council leader had simply been appointed by the supervisor.

Then a student from the college, introduced only as a visiting fellow, stood and said something that rearranged the room for Sophie. "Consider how a parliamentary system works," the fellow said. "The head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election." He sat down almost immediately, as if embarrassed to have taken the floor at all, and Ms. Boateng moved on to the next speaker.

Sophie wrote the sentence down in the margin of her index cards, the pen pressing hard enough to groove the card beneath. She read it twice. So nobody had voted directly for that prime minister on the television because nobody was supposed to; he kept his job only as long as the legislature still had confidence in him, and the day he lost it, he was out. In the presidential model she'd grown up lionizing in her civics notes, the president won a separate election and could not be removed that way, no matter what the legislature thought of him, at least not through an ordinary vote. Two different logics. One made the leader answerable continuously to the assembly; the other made him answerable to the voters on a fixed day, and only on that day.

When her turn came, Sophie stood and looked at her cards and then put them face down on the chair behind her. "I came here to argue for direct election," she said. "I thought it was the only legitimate way, because that's how we do it and we don't question it. But a prime minister isn't elected separately at all. He holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature. If he loses that confidence, he's gone, sometimes overnight." She heard her own voice steady in the borrowed silence of the gym. "So the question isn't which one is democratic. It's which kind of answerability we want. Do we want the youth council leader chosen by us once and hard to remove, or chosen by the council and easy to remove? I honestly don't know yet, and I think it's fine to say that out loud in a town hall."

Braelyn turned around in her seat and looked at her for a long second, then raised her hand. "Then amend it," Braelyn said when Ms. Boateng called on her. "Vote tonight on the amendment, and let Sophie be the one to move it." There was a scatter of laughter, some of it warm, and the older man near the stage muttered that at least somebody under thirty was paying attention.

Ms. Boateng found the amendment in her folder of prepared motions, and Sophie walked to the microphone at the side of the stage, unfolded the paper, and read the words proposing that the council leader serve at the confidence of the members, subject to removal by a simple vote. "All those in favor," Ms. Boateng said, and Sophie counted the raised hands along with everyone else, her pencil moving down the column she had drawn in the margin.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
The print of The Broken Column had been pinned to the art room wall for two weeks before Ms. Chaudhry made it the assignment, and Amelia had spent most of those two weeks avoiding it. Now she sat at the long table with her sketchbook open to a blank page, and the woman in the painting stared back at her, tears on her cheeks, metal corset buckled around her torso, nails driven into her skin.

"You have to pick a painting and do a formal analysis," Ms. Chaudhry had said that morning, tapping the wall with one finger. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Not whether you like it. Not how it makes you feel, at least not at first. What the painting is doing, and how."

Amelia wanted to do it well, and she also wanted to do it fast, because Mathew had already claimed the Kahlo and was three tables away writing with the smug, unhurried confidence of someone who had finished a draft. She watched him underline something twice. Then she went back to the painting, because the assignment said one painting per student and she had been left with a Monet she found pleasant and forgettable, a smear of arboreal green along a riverbank that gave her nothing to say.

The problem, she decided, was that Mathew was doing it wrong. She could hear him muttering to Alexandre across the tables.

"She's sad because of the accident," Mathew was saying. "Bus accident, spine injury, so the nails are the pain. Obviously."

"Obviously," Alexandre repeated, in a tone that suggested he thought it was not obvious at all. He was folding a gum wrapper into a tiny triangle. "But why is there architecture in her torso?"

Amelia looked up. "What?"

"In the painting," Alexandre said, tipping his chair back. "There's a column where her middle should be. Like a building. Why would a person have a building inside them?"

"Because her spine broke," Mathew said. "It's a metaphor."

"A metaphor for what, though," Alexandre said, and now Amelia was already out of her chair, because the question was better than anything she had written about Monet.

She stood in front of the print with her hands behind her back, the way Ms. Chaudhry stood when she was looking at something properly. The desert behind the figure was cracked earth, ochre and grey, a landscape with no shelter in it. The figure's skin was pale against that ground, and the column ran straight up through the opening in her body, white with ridges, broken near the middle with a clean gap where the pieces no longer met.

"It's an Ionic column," Amelia said, and then doubted herself immediately, because she had learned the orders in grade ten and might be confusing them. "The scroll at the top. That's Ionic. Doric is the plain one, Corinthian has the leaves."

"So a Greek column," Alexandre said, "is her spine. Inside her body."

"Through an opening in her body," Amelia said slowly, tracing the shape in the air, the split in the torso that let the viewer see it. "It's a cracked Ionic column, visible through an opening in her body. That's what it is, exactly."

Mathew came over, reluctant, still holding his draft like a shield. "That's what I said. Broken spine."

"No," Amelia said. "You said the nails mean pain. But the column is doing something different from the nails. The nails are all over her skin, outside, small, lots of them. The column is one thing, inside, structural. It's holding her up, or failing to hold her up. A column is what a building stands on." She heard herself accelerate and made herself slow down. "She painted herself as a building that's failing, and the only thing keeping her vertical is the thing that's broken."

The room had gone quieter around them. Ms. Chaudhry was at her desk, not looking up, which Amelia had learned meant she was listening.

"So it's not just sad," Alexandre said. "It's load-bearing sadness."

"Composition," Amelia said, grabbing her sketchbook and starting to write without sitting down. "The figure is vertical, front and centre, symmetrical, and the column is the vertical inside the vertical. The landscape is horizontal and torn. Everything horizontal in the painting is broken ground. The only intact axis is her, and even that has a crack in it."

"What about the sheet?" Mathew said, pointing at the lower half of the figure, where a white cloth wound around the hips. "I wrote it means vulnerability."

"Or it means she's an offering," Amelia said. "You lay things on cloth. I don't know. I genuinely don't know about the sheet."

Mathew looked at his draft and then at the painting, and she watched him cross out a line. It gave her a small, unworthy satisfaction, and she noted her own culpability in it, the way she had drifted over here partly to beat him rather than to understand, and she wrote that down too, in the margin, because it seemed like the kind of thing Ms. Chaudhry would want and because it was true.

"So can you switch?" Alexandre asked. "You clearly want the Kahlo."

"She'd have to convince Mathew to trade," Ms. Chaudhry said from the desk, finally looking up. "Or write about the Monet. Or, and this is the third option, share the painting and write two different analyses."

"Two analyses of the same painting," Mathew said, "that disagree."

"That happen to disagree," Ms. Chaudhry said. "You don't have to plan the disagreement. Just be honest about what you see and what you don't."

Mathew tore his draft in half, not dramatically, just folded it and tore it, and dropped both pieces on the table. "Fine," he said. "But I'm keeping the nails."

"Keep the nails," Amelia said. She pulled a chair over next to his and opened her sketchbook flat. "I get the column."

She looked once more at the print, at the gap in the white stone where the two halves of the spine failed to meet, at the face above it holding itself composed. Then she wrote her first sentence at the top of the page and pressed hard enough to dent the paper.

"Start here," she said, turning the sketchbook so Mathew could read it.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
Elijah had claimed the corner table by the window on the second floor of the public library, where the radiators clanked like a small animal trapped in the wall, and he had been sitting there for two hours with almost nothing to show for it. The assignment sheet lay between his elbow and a cold cup of vending machine hot chocolate. Write a historiographical essay, Ms. Virtanen had said, on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800. He understood each of those words separately. Together they were a locked door.

He had opened with Thomas Carlyle, because Carlyle came up first in the search results, all blood and drama and the guillotine rising like a bird of prey. It was exhilarating to read, in the way a storm is exhilarating from indoors, and he had written a page of it before noticing that the page said nothing about anyone's view changing. It was just noise about the Terror. He suspected his teacher would call it, in her neat red handwriting, colorful but gratuitous, and the thought made him put his head briefly on the table.

Mina found him there at four, dumping her bag on the chair across from him with the confidence of someone who believed all tables were partly hers. "You look like the Revolution already happened to you," she said.

"It kind of did." He turned his laptop so she could see the mess. "The essay's about how historians after 1800 argued with each other. Except I don't know what the first argument even was. Everyone after 1800 is responding to something, and I keep finding the responses without the thing."

Kayne arrived a minute later with a stack of books he was not going to read, which was his way of feeling scholarly. He flipped one open, looked at a footnote, and said, "There's a name in here that's in like every chapter. Burke. Edmund Burke. It says he wrote this book, Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790."

"That's before 1800," Mina said, as if Kayne had personally tried to sneak it past her. "Doesn't your essay start after 1800?"

"Maybe it doesn't matter that it's before," Elijah said slowly. He pulled the library catalogue toward him and typed the name. There was a copy, one shelf away, in the section with the smell of old paper and the lamps that only half worked. He went and got it himself, which felt different from downloading something, heavier in the hand.

He read the first pages standing between the stacks, and then he sat down on the carpeted step because standing seemed suddenly too active for what he was absorbing. Burke, writing while the Revolution was still young, had condemned it. Not for failing, but for succeeding at the wrong thing, for destroying tradition, tearing down an inheritance that should have been passed on rather than smashed. So that was the position. The conservative view, the footnote called it, the one historians after 1800 argued with, the fixed point everyone else pushed against or circled back to. His whole essay had been a conversation with the doors cut off. Now the doors were open, and he could see the shape of it: Burke on one side, and then two centuries of people taking sides.

Back at the table, he said it out loud to test it. "It's not that historians after 1800 all agreed. It's that they all had to deal with him first. He's the oldest voice in the room and nobody can leave the room."

"So your essay starts before the starting date," Kayne said. "Is that allowed?"

"It's my essay," Elijah said, and Mina laughed at the grandiosity of it, and he laughed too, and then he actually started writing, fast, the way you write when the argument has stopped being a puzzle and started being a road. He worked out his own position in the margin, half-formed and honest: that Burke was right that something was lost, and wrong about what was worth keeping, and that he, Elijah, sixteen, could hold both of those at once without pretending the balance was easy. It didn't resolve. He underlined a question he couldn't answer yet and left it in the margin like a door he'd come back to.

When Ms. Virtanen came through at closing, wheeling the return cart and pausing at their table, she picked up the Burke, looked at the due date slip, and raised an eyebrow at the pub date printed on the title page. "Heavy company for a Tuesday," she said.

"The heaviest," Elijah said. "He's a polymath. He wrote about aesthetics and politics and, like, everything." He closed the laptop, slid the book into his bag with the assignment sheet folded around it as a bookmark, and helped her stack Kayne's untouched pile onto the cart before following Mina down the stairwell, where the clanking radiator sounded, for once, almost like applause.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
story:
The credit union smelled like carpet cleaner and old paper, and Sara stood in line behind Abigaelle, holding both their bank slips because Abigaelle's hands were shaking too badly to hold anything. It was the third of the month. Rent had been due on the first.

"Sixty-two dollars," Abigaelle said, staring at the deposit screen as if the number might revise itself upward if she watched long enough. "I have sixty-two dollars and rent is five-forty. My mom said maybe next week, and next week is a lie my mom tells."

Sara did the arithmetic in her head and kept her face still. Outside, across the parking lot, a storefront with green neon letters said FAST CASH, NO HASSLE, and Abigaelle had looked at it twice on the walk in. There was a folded flyer in her jacket pocket; Sara had seen it on the bus, seen her unfold it and read it and fold it again, and neither of them had said anything about it.

When their number came up, the teller was an older woman with reading glasses on a chain, effusive in the way of someone who had been pleasant to strangers for thirty years and could no longer stop. She counted Abigaelle's deposit into the machine, and when Abigaelle asked, quietly, whether the credit union did short-term loans, the woman said they did small personal loans but there was an application, a day or two, a credit check. Abigaelle thanked her and turned away before the sentence was finished.

In the lobby, by the brochure rack, Sara took the flyer out of Abigaelle's pocket herself. "Fifteen dollars per hundred," she read. "You'd need five hundred, so what, seventy-five in fees?"

"For two weeks," Abigaelle said. "Then I pay it back when Mom's check comes."

Sara looked at the fine print, then at the ceiling, then at the flyer again, because something about the numbers was bothering her in a way she couldn't yet name. "My econ teacher made us read this thing from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau," she said slowly. "A typical payday loan fee, fifteen dollars per hundred borrowed for two weeks, works out to an annual percentage rate of almost four hundred percent."

"Almost four hundred percent of what?"

"That's the rate. If you annualize it. That's what the fee equals."

Abigaelle took the flyer back and held it against her chest. "It's two weeks. I'm not annualizing anything. I just need five hundred dollars until Friday."

The lobby went quiet around them. Sara thought about her own savings account, the one she'd opened at fourteen with birthday money, the teller's line about compound interest, how the money earned interest and the interest earned interest too, small and slow and going in the right direction. She thought about how the same word, interest, meant two opposite things depending on which side of the counter you stood on. "There's this," she said, and pulled out her phone and opened her banking app, and turned the screen so Abigaelle could see the balance, which was eight hundred and ten dollars. It was money for her first semester's textbooks, due at the college store in September. She had been guarding it since March with a discipline that both exhilarated and depressed her.

"That's your book money," Abigaelle said.

"I know what it is."

"You'd be a revisionist saint in five years, telling everyone how you lent me rent money."

"I'd be telling everyone how you paid me back."

"I'd pay you back."

"Then it's not a story."

They stood there while the line moved behind them and the neon sign burned green across the lot, and Sara watched her friend do the math in her own head, watched her lips move around almost four hundred percent the way you test a loose tooth. It was Abigaelle who finally spoke, and what she said made Sara's stomach drop, because it was not about the flyer at all.

"I didn't take one today," Abigaelle said. "I took one last Thursday."

Sara's hand was still out with the phone in it, the balance glowing. "For how much?"

"Three hundred. I was going to tell you when I paid it off." Abigaelle looked at the green sign through the glass doors, and then at the deposit slip in Sara's other hand, sixty-two dollars printed on it in fading ink. "The two weeks is up a week from tomorrow."

Sara put the phone back in her pocket, slowly, so the screen went dark against her leg. Then she picked up both their slips and walked back toward the teller window, and Abigaelle, after a moment, followed her.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
The gate to the community garden stuck, and Joshua had to lift it on its hinge the way Terry had shown him once, in April, when they were both there for a different reason. Back then it had been a punishment, six Saturdays of weeding after the incident with the parking lot and the shopping cart, and Joshua had resented every minute. Now he had signed up voluntarily to help the food bank that kept its pantry in the garden's little shed, and he could not quite explain to himself what had changed, except that something had, and he wanted to see it through.

Terry was already at the compost bins, elbow-deep, because Terry was always elbow-deep in something. "You came back," he said, not looking up. "I didn't think you would."

"Truck comes at noon," Joshua said. "Ms. Whitaker asked for extra hands."

At the far end of the plot, past the tomato cages and the rhubarb nobody ever wanted, the ground sloped down to a littoral strip of weedy mud along the creek, where discarded grocery carts went to rust. Ms. Whitaker was there, talking to a woman Joshua didn't know, a woman in an apron who kept glancing at her watch. He drifted close enough to hear.

"Forty loaves," the woman was saying. "That's what's left over from this morning, and I can't just throw it out, but if somebody gets sick, my insurance, my whole place."

Ms. Whitaker put a hand on the woman's shoulder. "The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996," she said. "That's what covers you."

The woman frowned. "Covers me how?"

"It gives you limited protection from liability when you donate. That's why stores and restaurants do it." Ms. Whitaker turned and saw Joshua. "There you are. We have bread coming and greens to cut, and the pantry opens at noon whether we're ready or not."

He followed her up the slope, and while she handed him shears and a crate she kept talking, but not to him exactly, more to the morning. She'd owned a diner for twenty-six years, she said, and every night she'd watched bread go into the bin out back because she'd been afraid, and only in her last year, when another owner told her about the law, had she started donating instead. "Twenty-five years of bread," she said. "You can do that arithmetic if you want. I've done it enough."

Joshua cut Swiss chard and thought about arithmetic. He thought about the parking lot, too, how he and Terry had ridden that cart down the slope toward the creek, and how it had clipped a stranger's bumper, and how his first instinct had been to say nothing until the coach had made him. Terry had taken half the blame without being asked, which had embarrassed Joshua more than the punishment. He hadn't acceded to that arrangement gracefully; he'd argued, said it wasn't Terry's fault, and Terry had shrugged and said it wasn't about fault, it was about what they were going to do next.

Francisco arrived at ten-thirty with a wagon, having been sent from the pantry to haul the crates. "Bread's here," he announced. "The apron lady. She's unloading at the curb."

They carried the loaves in together, and Joshua, stacking them on the shelf by date, found himself explaining to Francisco why the bread existed at all, the law, the limited protection, the way it made a diner owner willing to give away her surplus. Francisco listened, then said, "So she was scared for nothing."

"For twenty-five years," Joshua said.

Francisco whistled, which felt to Joshua like the right response, the only response, and they went back out for the greens.

By eleven-forty the crates were heavy and the sun had moved, and Ms. Whitaker called a pause. The three of them sat on the overturned cart by the shed, which someone had rescued from the creek years ago and never returned to any store. Joshua had a presentiment, sitting there, that he would remember this morning, though he couldn't have said what about it would matter, and he didn't trust the feeling. He'd had the same feeling the day of the cart, a sense that the afternoon was going to become a story he'd tell, and it had, but not the story he'd imagined.

"Can I ask you something," he said to Ms. Whitaker. "That bread you threw out. Would you really have donated it, if you'd known? Or is that just what you tell yourself now?"

She peeled an orange with her thumbnail, unhurried. "That's a fair question," she said. "I think I would have. But I said I'd done the arithmetic, not that I trusted the answer."

Terry laughed, and Francisco looked from one of them to the other, sensing something older than the morning. At noon a car pulled into the lot, then another, and a woman got out holding the hand of a kid in a dinosaur backpack. Ms. Whitaker stood, brushing orange peel from her jeans.

"All right," she said. "Doors open."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
story:
Sydney spread the two articles across the library table like a hand of cards she did not want to play. The first, from 2011, claimed that students who handwrote their notes outperformed students who typed them. The second, from 2016, found no difference at all. Mr. Swampy had assigned them as a pair on purpose, and the assignment sheet sat between the photocopied pages, asking for a critical review of eight hundred words that compared the studies and came to some considered position. She had been at the table for an hour and had written one sentence, which she had then crossed out so thoroughly that the paper had torn.

Gurshaan dropped into the chair opposite her with a granola bar and no apparent shame about the crumbs. "Still stuck?" he asked. He was writing about two studies on later school start times, a topic he described as a gift because both articles agreed. "Mine basically write themselves. Both of them say teenagers need more sleep. I just have to say which one proved it better."

"That's not comparing," Sydney said. "That's just agreeing twice." She turned the 2011 article toward him and pointed at the results table, then at the 2016 table, where the numbers sat flat and unimpressive. "This one says handwriting helps. This one says it doesn't. They used almost the same method. So which one do I believe?"

Judah arrived with his laptop already open, sliding into the third chair without pausing his typing. He was the fastest writer in their class and the most annoying, in Sydney's opinion, though she had never said so aloud. He glanced at her pages for exactly two seconds. "Pick the newer one," he said. "Science corrects itself. The 2016 one wins."

"But it doesn't say the first one was wrong. It just says nothing." Sydney sat back and looked at the ceiling tiles, which had the glacial gray of every school ceiling ever installed. Somewhere behind the reference desk, Mr. Swampy was reshelving with the patience of a man who had done it for decades. She thought of her mother, who had switched careers at forty and claimed the hardest part was admitting the first fifteen years had been a partial mistake. Sydney wondered whether it was harder to revise an opinion or to hold two conflicting ones in her head at the same time, suspended, without letting either one crash.

She started searching anyway, more to avoid writing than because she expected anything. Study after study came up. Handwriting beat typing. Handwriting beat typing again. A meta-analysis, even, pooling dozens of experiments, all pointing the same direction, and Sydney felt her shoulders relax. If everything agreed, the 2016 study was the outlier, the fluke, and her review could end there, tidy and defensible. She copied a citation into her notebook. Then she stopped, pen still touching the paper, because a small phrase in the meta-analysis's limitations section had caught her eye, a phrase about publication bias, about unpublished studies. She had skimmed past it the first time. She went back and read it properly, and then she typed new words into the search bar: unpublished, null, handwriting.

Gurshaan leaned over her shoulder. "What's a null result?"

"When they find nothing," Sydney said slowly, reading as she answered. "The effect isn't there." The search results were not the clean columns of the database she had been using. They were blogs, a statistics professor's page, a PDF with ugly formatting and no journal logo. She read a paragraph, then read it again. In 1979, a psychologist named Robert Rosenthal had given the thing a name.

"The file drawer problem," she said out loud, mostly to the table.

"The what?" Judah looked up from his screen for the first time.

"It's called the file drawer problem. Studies with null results go unpublished, sitting in someone's drawer, so the published record looks more positive than the evidence." She heard the sentence leave her mouth and felt something shift, the same shift she'd felt at thirteen when a dentist told her the pain in her jaw was coming from a tooth on the other side. Every article finding the handwriting effect might be only the visible fraction. The 2016 study, the one Judah had dismissed as the loser, might be one of the few honest zeros that had escaped the drawer. She could not know how many zeros existed. Nobody could, apparently. That was the point, and it was inconvenient, because it meant her review could not end in a winner.

She pulled the assignment sheet toward her and started a list, not of conclusions but of what she could actually claim. The 2011 study had a smaller sample. The 2016 study had used a more realistic classroom task. The meta-analysis was positive but possibly built on a tilted record. Beside each line she wrote the counterweight, and beside some of the counterweights she wrote question marks, because the question marks were honest. When Gurshaan asked what she would argue, she told him she did not know yet, that maybe arguing was the wrong word for what the essay should do. Maybe it should problematize the question instead, hold the two studies against each other and admit where the light ran out. He said that sounded like a way to lose marks. She said it might be.

Mr. Swampy passed their table on his slow circuit of the shelves and paused long enough to read the title of the 2011 article, upside down, without comment. After he moved on, Sydney wrote her opening sentence, a real one this time, then a second. Across from her, Judah had stopped typing and was staring at his own screen, his cursor blinking in an empty paragraph, and after a moment he said, quietly, "Both of mine agree. Why does that suddenly feel worse?"

story:
The community centre smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and the folding tables had been pushed into a rectangle in the corner of the gym. Hudson arrived early because Mr. Kang, who ran the Saturday civics seminar, had promised that anyone who came on time could claim the chair that didn't wobble. He claimed it. Then he set out his two workbooks, one on parliamentary systems and one on presidential, and waited for someone to argue with him.

Cailyn arrived second, holding her phone like evidence. "Okay, quiz me," she said, dropping into the chair across from him. "My mum's whole family is in Manchester. My nan called last night and she said, and I quote, that the country has gone completely round the bend." She turned the phone toward him. A message from her cousin filled the screen, tapped out at two in the morning UK time: "Hud, settle a bet. In 2022 we had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, then Liz Truss, then Rishi Sunak, and nobody voted. Not one of us. How is that even a country? Also, is it true American presidents can't be fired by their own party? Reply quick, Rex owes me a tenner."

Hudson read the message twice. Rex slid into the seat beside him before he could answer, already talking about how he'd read that a prime minister could just be replaced by the governing party whenever it felt like it, which to Rex proved that the whole British system was theater. "It's basically nihilism with a flag," Rex said. Hudson said that wasn't what nihilism meant, and Rex said it was close enough, and Mr. Kang knocked twice on the table and told them both to put up or shut up.

The exercise on the whiteboard read: compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government, then defend one to the room. Hudson had already filled two pages at home, and his first draft favored the presidential system because the voters knew exactly who they were getting and the removal process, impeachment, was deliberate and rare. But Cailyn's cousin's message sat in his mind like a splinter. Three prime ministers in a single year, Johnson and Truss and Sunak, changed without a general election, because the governing party changed its leader. He hadn't known that. His draft hadn't accounted for it at all.

"That's the point, though," Rex said when Hudson raised it. "The party can fix its own mistake fast. Your president gets elected and you're stuck for four years no matter what." Hudson started to answer and then stopped, because he could see both halves at once and they refused to be stacked into a ranking. In a parliamentary system, the head of government came out of the legislature and could fall with it, quick, responsive, but three prime ministers in one year without the voters weighing in looked like the public had been cut out of the loop entirely. In a presidential system, the mandate was plain and the removal bar was high, but high bars kept bad outcomes in place too. He wrote a line down the middle of his page and put each fact on its own side.

Cailyn texted her cousin back and held the reply where both boys could read it: "Nan says you're all soft, and Rex pays up, but also she says nobody's explained to her once why she never got a say." When Mr. Kang called the room to order and asked for a first defense, Hudson raised his hand, then put it down, then raised it again.

He stood at the whiteboard and said the honest version. "I came in preferring the presidential system, because it's cleaner. The country votes for one person, and that person can only be removed by impeachment, which almost never happens." He tapped the board. "But in 2022 the UK had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, and there was no general election at all. The governing party just changed its leader twice. Cailyn's family lived through it and nobody asked them." He paused. "I think the parliamentary system is faster when something goes wrong. I think the presidential system is more honest about who's in charge. I can't tell you which one I'd pick yet, and I don't want to pretend I can."

Rex said, "So you're abstaining," and made it sound like an accusation. Mr. Kang wrote Hudson's name on the board under a column headed "unresolved," and told the room it was the only column with anything in it. Cailyn slid a folded ten across the table toward Rex, who pocketed it without breaking eye contact. Hudson sat back down and, under the line dividing his page, added one more sentence, then turned the notebook so Cailyn could read it: "Ask your nan what she'd change."
